Cool slightly, blend smooth, then push through a sieve to leave the skins and seeds behind.
steps.tip: Sieving is what gives kut its velvety body — do not skip it.

steps.text: Heat 3 tbsp oil in a heavy pan, crackle the mustard, cumin and fenugreek, then add the curry leaves, dried red chillies and green chillies.
Add the crushed garlic and fry 1 minute until it smells sweet and turns pale gold, then take the pan off the heat and stir in the asafoetida.
steps.tip: Asafoetida burns almost instantly on a hot base — off the heat is the safe way.

steps.text: Return to the heat, add the chilli powder and coriander powder, and fry 20 seconds before pouring in the sieved tomato.
Whisk the standing besan slurry once more and pour it in slowly, stirring constantly. Simmer 12 minutes until the gravy is thick, glossy and no longer tastes of raw flour.
steps.tip: Pour the slurry in a thin stream while stirring, or you will be picking out lumps for the next ten minutes.

steps.text: Add the tamarind water and salt and simmer 5 minutes more; it should be thick enough to hold a channel behind the spoon.
Crack the eggs one at a time onto the surface, spacing them apart. Cover and poach on low for 6 minutes until the whites are set and the yolks still soft.
Heat the last 2 tbsp oil, sizzle a few extra curry leaves in it, and pour it over the top. Scatter with coriander leaves and serve with plain rice.

recipes.storage: The gravy keeps 3 days refrigerated, but poach the eggs fresh each time — reheated poached eggs go rubbery. Warm the kut with a splash of water over low heat, stirring so the besan does not catch.

recipes.name: Aab Gosht
recipes.subtitle: mutton chops poached in fennel-scented milk, pale and delicate

ingredients.note: aab gosht means water-meat, but milk is what carries it

ingredients.qty: 1 tbsp, tied in a square of muslin

ingredients.note: keeps the gravy pale where black pepper would speck it

prepNotes: Tie the fennel seeds in muslin so they can be fished out later; loose seeds in the finished gravy are unpleasant to eat.
Bring the milk to room temperature. Cold milk poured into a hot pan is the fastest way to make it catch.
Trim heavy fat off the chops — this dish should be delicate, and rendered fat makes the milk greasy.

steps.text: Bring the chops, water, garlic, bay leaf, both cardamoms, cloves, cinnamon, the muslin bag of fennel seeds and 1 tsp salt to a boil, then skim off the foam.
Simmer covered 45 minutes, until the meat is tender and pulling from the bone, then uncover and boil the liquid down to about 150ml.
steps.tip: Reducing the stock first concentrates the flavour; skip it and the milk simply dilutes everything.

steps.text: Remove the muslin bag and squeeze it out into the pan.
Add the milk in three additions, letting each come back to a bare simmer before the next goes in.
steps.tip: Three additions, and never a rolling boil. Milk added all at once and boiled hard will curdle around the meat.

steps.text: Stir in the fennel powder, dry ginger and white pepper.
Simmer uncovered on low for 25 minutes, stirring the base every few minutes with a flat spoon, until the gravy thinly coats the back of it.
steps.tip: Use a flat-ended spoon and scrape the base each time — milk scorches there long before you can smell it.

steps.text: Heat the ghee separately until it is nut-brown and pour it over the pan, giving it one stir.
Check the salt, rest 10 minutes off the heat and serve with plain rice or with a girda.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat on the lowest flame, stirring, and add a splash of milk to loosen; it will split if it boils.

recipes.name: Chaman Qaliya
recipes.subtitle: fried paneer in a thin turmeric-yellow gravy, mild and milky

ingredients.note: chaman is the Kashmiri word for paneer
this is what makes it yellow
use compounded-free hing to keep the dish gluten-free

prepNotes: Cut the paneer thick. Thin slices go leathery in the pan and there is nothing to be done about it afterwards.
Boil a small pan of lightly salted water and keep it warm — the fried paneer goes straight into it, which is the trick that keeps it soft.
Pat the paneer dry before frying or the mustard oil will spit.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil until it just smokes, then take it off the flame for 30 seconds to settle.
steps.tip: Unsmoked mustard oil tastes raw and sharp, and no amount of simmering fixes it later.

steps.text: Fry the paneer in batches over medium heat, 2 minutes a side, to a pale gold — no darker.
Slip each fried piece into the warm salted water and leave it there while you make the gravy.
steps.tip: Five minutes in warm salted water is what turns fried paneer soft again instead of rubbery.

steps.text: Pour off all but 3 tbsp of the oil, add the hing, bay leaf, cloves, cinnamon and cardamom and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Off the heat, stir in the turmeric, fennel powder and dry ginger.
Add the water and 1 tsp salt, bring to a boil and let it bubble 5 minutes so the spices lose their raw edge.
Lower the heat, pour in the milk and let it come back to a bare simmer.
steps.tip: Keep it below a boil once the milk is in, or the gravy will split into curds and whey.

steps.text: Drain the paneer and slide it in. Simmer 8 minutes, until the gravy is the thickness of pouring cream and pale yellow.
Finish with the black pepper and the spoon of ghee, and serve with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated; the paneer firms up in the cold, so reheat gently and give it 5 minutes in the hot gravy to soften again.

recipes.name: Choek Wangun
recipes.subtitle: fried aubergine in a sharp tamarind gravy, sour before it is hot

ingredients.qty: 500g small aubergines, quartered lengthways with the stems left on
ingredients.note: or two large ones cut into thick wedges
choek means sour, and this is the sour
use compounded-free hing to keep the dish gluten-free
rounds off the sourness without making it sweet

prepNotes: Soak a walnut-sized lump of tamarind in 100ml hot water for 15 minutes, then squeeze and strain it to get your 2 tbsp of thick pulp.
Salt the cut aubergine lightly and leave it 10 minutes, then pat dry. It absorbs noticeably less oil that way.
Leave the stems on the quarters — they hold the pieces together through frying and look right on the plate.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes, then drop the flame to medium.
Fry the aubergine quarters in batches, 4 minutes a side, until the skin is blistered and the flesh is collapsing. Lift out onto paper.
steps.tip: Fry in batches with space around each piece. Crowd the pan and they steam grey instead of browning.

steps.text: Pour off all but 3 tbsp of the oil, add the cumin seeds and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add the hing, wait 10 seconds for it to foam, then take the pan off the heat.
Stir in the chilli powder, turmeric, fennel powder and dry ginger off the flame for 20 seconds.
steps.tip: This is the step people burn. The pan is hotter than it looks after frying aubergine.

steps.text: Return to low heat, add the water, tamarind pulp, jaggery and 1 tsp salt, and simmer 6 minutes until the gravy darkens and thickens slightly.
Slide the fried aubergine back in and simmer uncovered 6 minutes, spooning gravy over rather than stirring.
steps.tip: Stirring at this point mashes the aubergine into the sauce; use a spoon and baste.

steps.text: Rest 10 minutes off the heat — it is better warm than hot — and serve with rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and the sourness settles in nicely. Serve at room temperature or warm through gently in a pan; do not microwave, which turns the aubergine watery.

recipes.name: Gushtaba
recipes.subtitle: pounded mutton meatballs poached in a white yogurt gravy, the closing course of wazwan

ingredients.qty: 600g boneless leg, minced twice and completely free of sinew

ingredients.note: praan, the small Kashmiri shallot
helps the mince bind and stay tender
for a softer, whiter finish

prepNotes: Traditionally the meat is pounded on a stone with a wooden mallet for half an hour. Twice-minced leg plus ten minutes of working the bowl by hand gets you close; a food processor makes it pasty rather than springy.
Trim out every strand of sinew before mincing. One thread is enough to split a ball open in the gravy.
Whisk the yogurt smooth and let it come to room temperature — an hour out of the fridge.

steps.text: Work the mince with 2 tbsp ghee, 1 tsp of the fennel powder, 1/2 tsp dry ginger, the ground green cardamom, black pepper, baking soda and 1 tsp salt for a full 10 minutes, until it turns pale, tacky and springy.
steps.tip: It is ready when a pinch stretches between your fingers instead of crumbling.

steps.text: Chill the mix 20 minutes, then wet your palms and roll 8 balls the size of a small orange, smoothing away every crack.
steps.tip: Any crack on the surface opens up during poaching.

steps.text: Heat the remaining ghee in a wide pan and cook the shallot on low for 6 minutes until soft and translucent.
steps.tip: Do not let the shallot colour — gushtaba gravy must stay white.

steps.text: Add the black cardamom, cloves and cinnamon, then the remaining fennel powder and dry ginger, and stir for 30 seconds.
Off the heat, whisk in the yogurt and the water, then return to a low flame and stir constantly until it reaches a bare simmer, about 8 minutes.
steps.tip: Constant stirring right up to the simmer is the only thing standing between you and a curdled gravy.

steps.text: Slide the meatballs in one at a time. Do not stir for the first 10 minutes — swirl the pan by its handle instead.
Simmer uncovered on low for 40 minutes, spooning gravy over the balls now and then, until they are firm and the gravy is the thickness of single cream.
Stir in the milk and crushed mint, season, and give it 5 minutes more.
Rest 10 minutes off the heat and serve one gushtaba per person with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated with the meatballs fully submerged in their gravy; reheat them in it over a low flame. Do not freeze — the yogurt gravy separates on thawing.

recipes.name: Haak
recipes.subtitle: kashmiri greens boiled whole in mustard oil, chilli and hing, served in their own broth

ingredients.qty: 500g, leaves stripped from the thick stalks
ingredients.note: stands in for haak, the broad Kashmiri collard; collard greens or spinach also work
Kashmiri long green chillies are mild — use fewer hot ones
use compounded-free hing to keep the dish gluten-free
keeps the leaves bright green; leave it out if you prefer

prepNotes: Wash the leaves in three changes of water — haak is grown in mud and grit hides in the folds.
Leave the leaves whole or torn in half. Haak is never finely chopped, and the broth it makes, haakh ras, is spooned over rice as part of the dish.
Get the pan and the oil properly hot before anything goes in; this cooks in under 20 minutes and there is no time to catch up.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a wide pan until it just begins to smoke, then take it off the heat for 20 seconds.
steps.tip: Smoking the oil first burns off the raw pungency. Skip it and the greens taste acrid.

steps.text: Add the hing and the slit chillies and let them sizzle for 15 seconds.
Pour in the water, add the salt and dry ginger, and bring to a hard boil.
Push the leaves in a handful at a time, letting each batch wilt before the next goes in, about 2 minutes in all.
Boil uncovered on high for 12 minutes, stirring twice, until the leaves are tender but still hold their shape.
steps.tip: Uncovered and on high is what keeps haak green; a lid turns it olive-brown within minutes.

steps.text: Stir in the baking soda if using, and taste — the broth should be well salted, since it is eaten with rice.
Serve immediately in a deep bowl with plenty of its broth, alongside plain rice.

recipes.storage: Eat the same day; haak dulls in colour and flavour overnight. If you must keep it, refrigerate up to 24 hours and reheat briefly, uncovered, over high heat.

recipes.name: Kashmiri Dum Aloo
recipes.subtitle: Fried baby potatoes finished in a yogurt gravy with fennel and dry ginger, no onion or garlic

ingredients.note: peeled, pricked all over
the colour of the dish depends on this

prepNotes: Kashmiri Pandit cooking uses no onion or garlic. Fennel and dry ginger carry the dish instead, which is why both are essential here.
Prick the potatoes deeply before frying. The holes are how the gravy gets inside during the dum stage.
Whisk the yogurt completely smooth and add it off the heat, stirring constantly, or it will split.

steps.text: Fry the pricked potatoes in hot oil until deep golden and crusted all over, 8-10 minutes. Drain. They should be cooked through but firm.
Whisk the yogurt with the Kashmiri chilli, fennel powder and dry ginger until there are no lumps. Keep it beside the stove.
Heat the ghee in a heavy pan, add the asafoetida, cardamom, cinnamon and cloves, and let them bloom for 20 seconds.
Take the pan off the heat. Pour in the yogurt mixture, stirring without stopping. Return to low heat and keep stirring until it comes to a bare simmer and thickens slightly, about 5 minutes.
steps.tip: Constant motion and low heat are what stop yogurt splitting.

steps.text: Add the potatoes and salt with about half a cup of hot water. Cover tightly and cook on the lowest possible heat for 15-20 minutes, shaking the pan occasionally.
Uncover; the gravy should cling to the potatoes and the fat should show at the edges. Rest 10 minutes before serving.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and the flavour deepens. Do not freeze; the potatoes turn grainy and the yogurt separates. Reheat over low heat with a splash of water.

recipes.name: Kashmiri Pulav
recipes.subtitle: Mildly sweet saffron rice with fruit and nuts, served alongside the wazwan

ingredients.note: to finish

prepNotes: The sweetness should be barely there — this is a foil for rich meat dishes, not a dessert. One teaspoon of sugar for two cups of rice is enough.
Warm the saffron in the milk for ten minutes before using; dropping threads into the pot does almost nothing.

steps.text: Warm the milk and steep the saffron in it.
Fry the nuts and raisins in ghee until the nuts colour and the raisins puff. Lift out and reserve.
In the same ghee, bloom the whole spices, then add the drained rice and turn it gently for 2 minutes.
steps.tip: Gently — soaked grains break easily.

steps.text: Add the saffron milk, 2.5 cups water, sugar and salt. Bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat 12 minutes.
Rest, covered and off the heat, a further 10 minutes before lifting the lid.
Fork through the fried nuts and raisins and scatter pomegranate over the top.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat covered with a splash of water. Add the pomegranate fresh rather than storing it in the rice.

recipes.name: Kashmiri Rajma
recipes.subtitle: small dark kidney beans simmered with fennel and dry ginger, without an onion in sight

ingredients.note: the small dark beans of Bhaderwah if you can find them; they cook softer and sweeter
use compounded-free hing to keep the dish gluten-free

prepNotes: Soak the beans in plenty of cold water for at least 8 hours, or overnight. Unsoaked rajma will not soften however long you cook it.
Do not add salt until the beans are completely tender — salted water toughens the skins and adds half an hour to the cooking.
Soak the Kashmiri chilli powder in 4 tbsp warm water for 10 minutes; it goes in as a smooth paste and colours the gravy evenly.

steps.text: Boil the drained beans in the water with the bay leaf, black cardamom, cloves and cinnamon.
Simmer covered 60 minutes, or pressure-cook 20 minutes at full pressure, until a bean crushes to paste between finger and thumb.
steps.tip: Under-done rajma tastes chalky and no amount of gravy hides it. Test three beans, not one.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a second pan until it just smokes, then lower the flame.
steps.tip: Smoke the mustard oil first; raw, it stays bitter right through the dish.

steps.text: Add the hing and let it foam for 10 seconds.
Off the heat, stir in the chilli paste, turmeric, fennel powder and dry ginger, then return to low heat and fry for 2 minutes until the oil separates at the edges.
Pour the tempering into the beans along with their cooking liquid and add salt to taste.
Crush a ladleful of the beans against the side of the pot and stir them back in to thicken the gravy.
steps.tip: This is what gives Kashmiri rajma its body — there is no cream and no tomato doing that job.

steps.text: Simmer uncovered 15 minutes, until the gravy is red-brown and coats the beans rather than pooling around them.
Stir in the garam masala, rest 5 minutes and serve with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and is better on day two. Freezes well for a month; reheat with a splash of water to loosen the gravy.

recipes.name: Modur Pulav
recipes.subtitle: sweet saffron rice with milk, ghee and dried fruit, made for pandit feast days

ingredients.qty: a generous pinch, soaked in 2 tbsp warm milk

ingredients.note: Kashmiri apricots if you have them
sounds wrong in a sweet dish; it is what stops it tasting flat

prepNotes: Soak the rice 30 minutes and drain it well in a sieve for another 10 — wet grains steam into a clump instead of staying separate.
Soak the saffron in warm, not hot, milk for at least 20 minutes so the colour comes out fully.
Have the nuts fried and set aside before the rice goes in; the last stage moves quickly.

steps.text: Heat 3 tbsp of the ghee and fry the almonds and cashews until pale gold, about 90 seconds, then lift them out.
Fry the raisins in the same ghee for 15 seconds, until they puff up, and lift them out too.
steps.tip: Fifteen seconds is the whole window. Raisins go from plump to bitter and black very fast.

steps.text: Add the remaining ghee, then the cinnamon, cloves, cardamom and bay leaf, and let them scent the fat for 30 seconds.
Tip in the drained rice and turn it gently for 2 minutes, until every grain is coated and looks glassy at the edges.
steps.tip: Use a flat spatula and fold rather than stir; broken grains turn the pulav sticky.

steps.text: Pour in the water, milk, salt and the saffron milk, and bring to a boil.
As soon as it boils, lower the flame to its minimum, cover tightly and cook 12 minutes without lifting the lid.
Uncover, scatter over the sugar, fried nuts, raisins and apricot, and fold through with two strokes.
steps.tip: Sugar goes in only after the rice is cooked — add it earlier and the grains stay hard.

steps.text: Cover again and leave on the lowest heat for 5 minutes, then rest off the heat for 10 before serving warm.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat covered with a sprinkle of water, or steam for 5 minutes; a microwave dries the grains out.

recipes.name: Muji Gaad
recipes.subtitle: winter fish and radish in a red chilli gravy, sour and warming

ingredients.qty: 600g firm river fish, cut into 3cm steaks
ingredients.note: rohu or trout, bone in — the bone holds the piece together

ingredients.qty: 400g, peeled and cut into thick batons
ingredients.note: muj, the long white winter radish
use compounded-free hing to keep the dish gluten-free
the traditional souring; 1 tbsp tamarind pulp is a fair stand-in

prepNotes: Rub the fish steaks with 1 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp of the turmeric and leave them 15 minutes, then pat them thoroughly dry. Wet fish tears the moment it hits hot oil.
Muji gaad is a winter dish and it is meant to be eaten the day the fish is cooked — buy the fish the same morning if you can.
Soak the Kashmiri chilli in 3 tbsp warm water for 10 minutes so it goes in as a paste.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a wide pan until it smokes, then lower the flame to medium.
steps.tip: Fish will stick to anything less than properly hot oil in a properly hot pan.

steps.text: Fry the fish steaks in a single layer, 3 minutes a side, until crusted and deep gold. Lift them out and set aside.
steps.tip: Leave them alone for the full 3 minutes; a piece that resists the spatula is not ready to turn.

steps.text: Add the radish batons to the same oil and fry 5 minutes, until the edges brown and the sharp raw smell fades.
Add the hing and let it foam for 10 seconds.
Off the heat, stir in the chilli paste, remaining turmeric, fennel powder and dry ginger.
steps.tip: Kashmiri chilli scorches in a hot pan and takes the whole gravy brown with it.

steps.text: Pour in the water, add 1 tsp salt, and simmer covered 12 minutes until the radish is tender and the gravy has turned deep red.
Return the fish, add the crushed anardana, and simmer uncovered 8 minutes, spooning gravy over rather than stirring.
Rest 5 minutes off the heat and serve with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Best eaten the day it is made. It keeps 24 hours refrigerated; reheat covered over low heat without stirring, so the fish stays in pieces.

recipes.name: Mutton Yakhni
recipes.subtitle: pale yogurt and fennel mutton curry, aromatic rather than hot

ingredients.qty: 700g on the bone, cut into 4cm pieces
ingredients.note: shoulder or leg; the bone makes the stock
the backbone of the dish
sonth, not fresh ginger
use compounded-free hing to keep the dish gluten-free

ingredients.qty: 1 tbsp dried, crushed between the palms

prepNotes: Whisk the yogurt with 2 tbsp water until there is not a single lump, and leave it on the counter for 30 minutes. Cold, grainy yogurt splits the moment it meets a hot pan.
This is Kashmiri Pandit cooking: no onion, no garlic. Everything rests on fennel, dry ginger and a pinch of hing, so use fresh stock of all three — year-old fennel powder tastes of dust.
Take the mutton out of the fridge 30 minutes ahead so it does not seize when it hits the ghee.

steps.text: Bring the mutton, water, bay leaves, black cardamom, cloves, cinnamon and 1 tsp salt to a boil, then skim off every bit of grey foam.
steps.tip: Skim properly now or the finished yakhni will be cloudy instead of ivory.

steps.text: Cover and simmer 40 minutes, until the meat gives easily to a fork. Lift the pieces out and keep the strained stock.
Heat the ghee in a heavy pan and add the hing — it foams and smells sharp for about 10 seconds.
Pull the pan off the heat and stir in the fennel powder and dry ginger for 20 seconds.
steps.tip: Off the heat: ground fennel scorches in seconds and turns bitter.

steps.text: Return to a low flame, add the drained mutton and turn it in the spiced ghee for 3 minutes until every piece is glossy.
Take the pan off the heat again, pour in the whisked yogurt and stir without stopping for 2 minutes before setting it back on the lowest flame.
steps.tip: Keep stirring in one direction until the yogurt is hot through; stop early and it breaks into grains you cannot rescue.

steps.text: Add 450ml of the reserved stock, the crushed mint and the black pepper, and simmer uncovered 20 minutes until the gravy thinly coats a spoon.
Crush the green cardamom over the top, check the salt and rest 10 minutes off the heat before serving with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and tastes better on the second day. Reheat on the lowest possible flame while stirring; a hard boil will split the yogurt.

recipes.name: Nadru Yakhni
recipes.subtitle: lotus stem rounds in a gentle fennel and yogurt gravy, the meatless yakhni

ingredients.note: scrub the mud out of the hollows and slice into coins
use compounded-free hing to keep the dish gluten-free

prepNotes: If you are using real lotus stem, split each length open and rinse the hollow channels under a running tap — silt sits inside and no amount of surface washing reaches it.
Whisk the yogurt with 2 tbsp water until smooth and let it stand out of the fridge for 30 minutes so it does not split.
Cut the rounds thick, about 1cm. Thin slices go soft and disappear into the gravy.

steps.text: Boil the rounds in the water with the bay leaf, cloves, cinnamon and 1/2 tsp salt for 12 minutes, until a knife goes in with slight resistance.
steps.tip: Slight resistance, not soft — they will cook on in the gravy.

steps.text: Drain, keeping every drop of the cooking water.
Heat the ghee in a heavy pan and add the hing, letting it foam for 10 seconds.
Off the heat, stir in the fennel powder and dry ginger for 20 seconds.
steps.tip: Ground fennel scorches almost instantly on a hot base; take the pan off the flame first.

steps.text: Return to low heat, add the drained rounds and turn them for 3 minutes until coated.
Take the pan off the heat, pour in the yogurt and stir continuously for 2 minutes before setting it back on the lowest flame.
steps.tip: Do not walk away here. Yogurt that is heated without stirring curdles into grains.

steps.text: Add 350ml of the reserved cooking water, the cardamom, mint and black pepper, and simmer uncovered 15 minutes until the gravy just coats the rounds.
Check the salt and rest 5 minutes off the heat before serving with rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat over the lowest flame with a splash of water, stirring — boiling will break the yogurt.

recipes.name: Phirni
recipes.subtitle: chilled ground-rice pudding set in earthenware, scented with cardamom and rose

ingredients.qty: 60g, soaked 30 minutes then drained and coarsely ground
ingredients.note: grind to the texture of semolina, not to flour

ingredients.qty: a good pinch, soaked in 1 tbsp warm milk

ingredients.note: use one or the other, not both

prepNotes: Soak the rice 30 minutes, drain it thoroughly, then pulse it in a grinder to a coarse grit. Flour gives you a gluey paste; whole grains never soften.
Chill four shallow earthenware bowls, or any small bowls, before you pour. Phirni is set and served cold, never warm.
Soak the saffron in warm milk for 20 minutes so the colour and scent come out.

steps.text: Bring the milk to a boil in a heavy-based pan, then lower the heat to a bare simmer.
steps.tip: Heavy-based only. Milk catches on a thin pan and the burnt taste goes right through the dish.

steps.text: Mix the ground rice with 4 tbsp cold milk to a smooth slurry with no lumps.
steps.tip: Always slurry it cold first. Dry ground rice tipped into hot milk seizes into lumps immediately.

steps.text: Pour the slurry into the simmering milk in a thin stream, whisking the whole time.
Cook on low for 20 minutes, stirring constantly and scraping the base and corners, until the mixture coats the back of a spoon and the rice has no bite left.
steps.tip: Constant stirring for the full 20 minutes is the job. Stop for two minutes and it sticks.

steps.text: Add the sugar and cook 5 minutes more, until it thickens again to the consistency of pouring cream.
Stir in the saffron milk and the ground cardamom, and take the pan off the heat.
Let it cool for 5 minutes, then stir in the rose water or kewra.
steps.tip: Off the heat and slightly cooled — added to a boiling pan the scent simply evaporates.

steps.text: Pour into the chilled bowls while still pourable; it thickens a great deal as it sets.
Scatter with the slivered pistachios and almonds and refrigerate at least 4 hours until firm and cold.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days covered in the fridge and is meant to be eaten cold, straight from the bowl. Never reheat it — it is a set pudding, not a hot one.

recipes.name: Rista
recipes.subtitle: the red twin of gushtaba, meatballs poached in a chilli and fennel gravy

ingredients.qty: 600g boneless leg, minced twice and trimmed of all sinew

ingredients.note: for colour more than heat; this is what makes rista red
use compounded-free hing to keep the dish gluten-free
helps the mince hold together

prepNotes: Mince the leg twice and pick out every strand of sinew — rista balls poach for the best part of an hour and a single thread will unravel one.
Soak the Kashmiri chilli powder in 4 tbsp warm water for 10 minutes before you start. The paste gives an even red rather than gritty specks.
Chill the shaped balls for 20 minutes before they go into the pan; cold meat holds its shape far better.

steps.text: Work the mince with 2 tbsp ghee, 1 tsp fennel powder, 1/2 tsp dry ginger, the ground green cardamom, black pepper, baking soda and 1 tsp salt for 10 minutes until pale and springy.
steps.tip: Ten minutes of hand-working is what makes the texture; five minutes is not enough.

steps.text: Wet your palms and roll 8 smooth balls, slightly flattened, then chill them 20 minutes.
Heat the remaining ghee in a wide pan, add the hing and let it foam for 10 seconds.
Add the bay leaf, black cardamom, cloves and cinnamon and let them crackle for 30 seconds.
Off the heat, stir in the soaked chilli paste along with the rest of the fennel powder and dry ginger.
steps.tip: Off the heat, always — Kashmiri chilli burns fast and a scorched batch goes brown and bitter.

steps.text: Pour in the water, add 1 tsp salt and bring to a gentle boil, then let it bubble 5 minutes so the raw chilli taste cooks out.
Lower the balls in one by one and leave the pan alone for 10 minutes, swirling rather than stirring.
Simmer uncovered on low for 35 minutes, basting the balls with gravy, until the fat rises red on the surface and the gravy has reduced by a third.
steps.tip: That film of red fat on top is the sign it is done; without it the gravy still tastes raw.

steps.text: Rest 10 minutes off the heat and serve with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and deepens in colour overnight. Reheat gently with a splash of water; the meatballs freeze in their gravy for a month.

recipes.name: Rogan Josh
recipes.subtitle: Kashmiri lamb in a red gravy coloured by ratan jot and Kashmiri chilli, without onion or garlic

image.alt: A Kashmiri wazwan spread, in which rogan josh is served

ingredients.note: the colour comes from here, not from heat

prepNotes: Kashmiri Pandit cooking uses no onion or garlic at all. Fennel and dry ginger do that work, which is why both are in tablespoons here rather than teaspoons.
The red is from Kashmiri chilli and traditionally ratan jot (alkanet root), not from tomato — there is no tomato in this dish.

steps.text: Heat the ghee and bloom the asafoetida and whole spices until fragrant.
Add the mutton and sear over high heat until browned on all sides.
Take the pan off the heat. Stir the Kashmiri chilli, fennel and dry ginger into the whisked yogurt, then add it to the meat, stirring constantly.
steps.tip: Off the heat and constant motion — this is where yogurt splits.

steps.text: Return to low heat and cook, stirring, until the gravy thickens and the fat begins to show, about 10 minutes.
Add a cup of hot water and salt, cover, and simmer 60-70 minutes until the meat is tender and the gravy is deep red and glossy.
Rest 15 minutes. Serve with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and improves overnight. Freezes 2 months; the yogurt-based gravy can look grainy on thawing but comes back together when reheated slowly.

recipes.name: Tabak Maaz
recipes.subtitle: lamb ribs simmered soft in spiced milk, then fried crisp in ghee

ingredients.qty: 800g breast ribs, cut into flat pieces of two or three bones
ingredients.note: ask for the rib rack, not chops
use compounded-free hing to keep the dish gluten-free

prepNotes: Ask the butcher for the rib rack cut into flat two- or three-bone pieces about 10cm long. Chops will not do — tabak maaz is about the flat, crisp-edged slab.
The simmered ribs must cool and dry before they are fried. Cook them a few hours ahead, or the night before, and they will crisp far better.
Have a plate lined with kitchen paper ready; the ribs go straight from the ghee onto it.

steps.text: Put the ribs in a wide pan with the milk, water, turmeric, fennel powder, dry ginger, hing, both cardamoms, cloves, cinnamon, bay leaf and 1 tsp salt.
Bring to a bare simmer and hold it there, uncovered, for about 60 minutes.
steps.tip: Never let the milk reach a rolling boil — it catches on the base and the whole pot tastes scorched.

steps.text: The ribs are ready when the meat has shrunk back from the bone ends and almost all the liquid has gone, leaving a thick coating.
Lift the ribs onto a rack and leave them to cool and dry for at least 30 minutes.
steps.tip: Frying them wet means spitting ghee and a soggy, pale finish.

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a heavy frying pan over medium heat until it shimmers.
Fry the ribs in a single layer, 4 minutes on the first side, until the edges are deep gold and audibly crisp.
Turn once and give them 3 minutes on the second side, pressing lightly with a spatula so the whole face colours.
steps.tip: Turn once only. Repeated flipping tears the meat away from the bone.

steps.text: Drain on paper, scatter with salt and the black pepper, and serve hot as a starter with green chutney or plain.

recipes.storage: Best eaten within an hour of frying. The simmered, unfried ribs keep 2 days refrigerated in their reduced milk — fry them to order rather than reheating fried ones.

recipes.name: Ada Pradhaman
recipes.subtitle: rice ada simmered in jaggery and thick coconut milk, the sadya finale

ingredients.note: for homemade ada; use 200g shop-bought ada instead if you have it
dark and soft
500ml thin, 300ml thick
traditional, and it works

prepNotes: To make ada: knead the rice flour with boiling water and a pinch of salt into a stiff dough, spread it paper-thin on a greased banana leaf or foil, steam 8 minutes, cool and cut into 1cm squares. Shop-bought dried ada is entirely acceptable.
Soak dried shop-bought ada in hot water for 20 minutes, then drain and rinse under cold water so it stops sticking to itself.
Melt the jaggery separately in 1/2 cup water and strain it. Jaggery carries grit and you do not want it in the payasam.

steps.text: Boil the ada squares in plenty of water for 5 minutes until soft and translucent. Drain and rinse in cold water.
steps.tip: Rinsing washes off surface starch. Skip it and the payasam turns gluey.

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp ghee in a heavy pan and fry the cashews until golden, then the raisins until they puff, then the coconut slivers until brown. Lift each out separately.
steps.tip: Cashews burn while you fish out the raisins — do them one at a time.

steps.text: In the same pan pour in the strained jaggery syrup and boil 4 minutes until it thickens and coats a spoon.
Add the drained ada and cook in the syrup on low for 10 minutes, stirring, until each piece is glossy and has darkened to the colour of the jaggery.
steps.tip: This step is what makes ada pradhaman rather than sweetened coconut milk. Do not rush it.

steps.text: Pour in the thin coconut milk and simmer gently for 20 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until it reduces by about a quarter.
Stir in the remaining 2 tbsp ghee and cook 3 minutes more.
Add the powdered cardamom, dry ginger, cumin powder and the pinch of salt.
steps.tip: The salt and dry ginger are not optional flourishes — they are what stop it tasting flatly sweet.

steps.text: Take the pan off the heat and stir in the thick coconut milk. Do not return it to the boil.
steps.tip: Boiling after the thick milk goes in will split it. Off the heat, always.

steps.text: Scatter over the fried cashews, raisins and coconut slivers and serve warm.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and thickens into a pudding. Reheat over low heat with a little extra thin coconut milk; never boil it or the milk will separate.

recipes.name: Appam
recipes.subtitle: Lacy fermented rice pancakes with a soft, thick centre

ingredients.note: helps the batter ferment and spread
feeds the ferment

prepNotes: Appam batter ferments like dosa batter but is thinner and sweeter. It should pour, not spread.
The pan matters: a deep, round-bottomed appachatti is what makes the edges lacy and the centre thick. A small wok is the closest substitute.

steps.text: Grind the soaked rice with the grated coconut, cooked rice and enough water to make a smooth, pourable batter.
Add sugar, cover, and leave to ferment 8-10 hours until risen and faintly sour.
Stir in the coconut milk and salt. The batter should be thinner than dosa batter — like single cream.
steps.tip: Too thick and you get a pancake; too thin and it will not hold a centre.

steps.text: Heat the appachatti, wipe with coconut oil, pour a ladle into the middle, then immediately lift the pan and swirl it once so batter climbs the sides.
Cover and cook 2-3 minutes on low. Do not flip.
steps.tip: The lid is what steams the thick centre while the edges crisp.

steps.text: Lift out when the edges lift away on their own. Serve with stew, kadala curry or sweetened coconut milk.

recipes.storage: Batter keeps 3 days refrigerated and grows more sour; older batter suits appam less well than dosa. Cooked appams do not keep.

recipes.name: Avial
recipes.subtitle: Mixed vegetables bound in coconut, cumin and yogurt, finished with raw coconut oil

image.alt: An Onam sadya, the feast avial belongs to

ingredients.note: the Kerala vellarikka
2 for cooking, 1 raw at the end

prepNotes: Everything is cut to the same baton shape and size so it cooks evenly and looks right — this is not a dish where you cube things.
The final spoon of raw coconut oil is not optional. It is the smell of avial.

steps.text: Cook the vegetables hardest-first in a wide pan with turmeric, salt and just enough water — yam and banana first, softer vegetables after.
steps.tip: Barely enough water. Avial is not a curry and should not be swimming.

steps.text: Coarsely grind the coconut with cumin and green chilli. Do not make it a smooth paste.
steps.tip: Coarse. The texture of avial comes from the ground coconut.

steps.text: Fold the coconut mixture through the cooked vegetables and simmer 5 minutes.
Take the pan off the heat, then stir in the whisked yogurt. Return briefly to very low heat but do not let it boil.
steps.tip: Boiling after the yogurt goes in will split it.

steps.text: Crush the curry leaves between your palms and stir them in with the raw coconut oil.
Rest 10 minutes before serving. Avial is served warm, not hot.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat very gently — the yogurt splits over direct heat. Do not freeze.

recipes.name: Beef Ularthiyathu
recipes.subtitle: slow-fried beef in dark pepper masala with coconut slivers and a raft of curry leaves

ingredients.note: chuck or shin, with some fat
not grated — slivers
Kerala meat masala if you have it
a genuinely large amount

prepNotes: Marinate the beef 30 minutes with the turmeric, chilli powder, coriander powder, half the pepper, the vinegar and salt.
Ularthiyathu means roasted or fried down. The dish is finished when the gravy has gone entirely and the meat is coated in dark clinging masala — budget the time for it.
Slice the coconut into slivers rather than grating it. Grated coconut disappears; slivers stay and go crunchy.

steps.text: Pressure cook the marinated beef with 1/2 cup water and the whole cloves and cinnamon for 4 whistles, then 15 minutes on low. Release naturally.
steps.tip: If the beef is still chewy, give it 2 more whistles now. You cannot fix tough meat in the frying stage.

steps.text: Meanwhile, heat 2 tbsp coconut oil in a wide kadhai and fry the coconut slivers over medium heat for 3 minutes until golden. Lift out and set aside.
In the same oil add the shallots, ginger, garlic and green chillies. Cook 8 minutes until the shallots are deep brown at the edges.
Add the fennel powder, garam masala and remaining pepper and fry 1 minute until the oil smells of fennel.
Tip in the cooked beef along with any liquid from the cooker. Raise the heat and boil hard, stirring, for 8-10 minutes until the liquid has gone.
Add the remaining 2 tbsp coconut oil and turn the heat to medium-low. Now fry the beef, stirring every couple of minutes, for 20-25 minutes.
steps.tip: This is the whole dish. The meat should go from brown to near-black and the masala should look dry and crusted.

steps.text: Scrape the crust off the base of the pan back into the meat every few minutes — that is where the flavour is.
steps.tip: If it catches too hard, a tablespoon of water will lift it. Let it dry again before adding more.

steps.text: Throw in all four sprigs of curry leaves and the fried coconut slivers. Fry 2 minutes more until the leaves crisp and shatter.
Rest off the heat 5 minutes and serve with kappa or porotta.

recipes.storage: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and is better on day two. Reheat in a dry pan over medium heat for 5 minutes to bring the crust back; it will not need extra oil.

recipes.name: Cabbage Thoran
recipes.subtitle: shredded cabbage tossed with crushed coconut, mustard and curry leaves

ingredients.note: about half a medium head
small Kerala shallots if you can get them
goes into the coconut crush
crushed with the coconut

prepNotes: Shred the cabbage as thin as you can — thick shreds steam into limp ribbons instead of staying crisp.
Crush the coconut, garlic, cumin, turmeric and one green chilli together coarsely in a mortar. Do not run it in a blender; you want a rough crumble, not a paste.
Have everything ready by the stove. Thoran is done in fifteen minutes and the tempering waits for nobody.

steps.text: Heat the coconut oil in a kadhai over medium heat until it thins and shimmers.
Add the mustard seeds and let them pop, about 30 seconds, then add the broken red chillies and curry leaves.
steps.tip: Cover with a lid or a spatter guard — the leaves will crackle hard.

steps.text: Stir in the chopped shallot and remaining slit chillies. Cook 3 minutes until the shallot turns translucent and smells sweet.
Tip in the cabbage and salt. Toss to coat in the oil.
Cover and cook on low for 5 minutes. The cabbage will release its own water — do not add any.
steps.tip: Water is the enemy here. Thoran should be dry, not stewed.

steps.text: Uncover, raise the heat and stir-fry 2 minutes to drive off the moisture at the bottom of the pan.
Add the crushed coconut mixture and toss through for 2 minutes, until the coconut smells toasty and looks dry.
Taste for salt and take it off the heat while the cabbage still has bite.
steps.tip: Overcooked thoran goes grey and sulphurous. Stop early.

recipes.storage: Best the day it is made. Keeps 2 days refrigerated; revive in a hot dry pan for 2 minutes rather than a microwave, which makes it watery.

recipes.name: Chemmeen Manga Curry
recipes.subtitle: prawns and raw mango in a sharp red coconut gravy from the backwaters

ingredients.note: medium sized, tails on

ingredients.qty: 1 small, peeled and cut into thick slices
ingredients.note: sour, firm and green
200ml thin, 100ml thick
whole seeds

prepNotes: Toss the prawns with 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt and leave 15 minutes while you build the gravy.
Taste the raw mango first. If it is only mildly sour, use the whole fruit; if it is fiercely sour, use half and top up with a squeeze of lemon at the end.
This curry is cooked in a manchatti (clay pot) traditionally, which is why the gravy is thin and clings. Any heavy shallow pan works — just keep it wide.

steps.text: Heat the coconut oil in a wide pan and pop the mustard seeds, about 30 seconds.
Add the fenugreek seeds and let them darken for 15 seconds only.
steps.tip: Fenugreek turns bitter the moment it goes past golden brown. Count it out.

steps.text: Add the shallots, ginger, garlic, green chillies and 2 sprigs of curry leaves. Cook 6 minutes until the shallots are soft and just starting to colour.
Turn the heat to low, add the Kashmiri chilli and turmeric and fry 45 seconds until the oil runs red.
steps.tip: Low heat here or the chilli scorches and the whole curry tastes acrid.

steps.text: Add the mango slices, the thin coconut milk and salt. Simmer 8 minutes until the mango is tender but still holding together.
Slide in the prawns and cook 3-4 minutes, just until they turn opaque and curl into loose C shapes.
steps.tip: A tightly curled O means overcooked and rubbery. Pull them at the C.

steps.text: Stir in the thick coconut milk and the last sprig of curry leaves. Warm through 1 minute without boiling.
Take off the heat and rest covered for 10 minutes so the mango sourness spreads through the gravy.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated, though the prawns firm up. Reheat gently without boiling; the sourness is stronger on day two, so a splash of coconut milk balances it.

recipes.name: Idiyappam
recipes.subtitle: steamed rice string hoppers, soft and threadlike, served with coconut milk

ingredients.note: boiling
for greasing the plates and hands

prepNotes: You need an idiyappam press (sevanazhi) with the finest disc. A potato ricer with a fine plate will do at a push.
If your rice flour is not pre-roasted, dry-roast it on low for 6-8 minutes until warm and fragrant without colouring, then cool.
Work the dough while it is hot — hot enough to be just bearable. Cold dough will not extrude and comes out as broken worms.

steps.text: Bring the water to a full rolling boil with the salt and 1 tsp of the coconut oil.
Pour the boiling water over the rice flour all at once, stirring hard with a wooden spoon until it comes together as a shaggy mass.
steps.tip: All at once, not gradually. Half-scalded flour makes a dough that cracks.

steps.text: Cover and rest 5 minutes so the flour absorbs fully.
Oil your palms and knead the warm dough for 3-4 minutes until it is completely smooth, soft and non-sticky — like fresh play dough.
steps.tip: If it cracks when rolled, sprinkle in a tablespoon of hot water and knead again.

steps.text: Grease the idiyappam plates and scatter a teaspoon of grated coconut on each.
Load the press and squeeze the dough onto the plates in tight overlapping spirals, about 1cm thick.
Scatter a little more coconut on top and stack the plates in a steamer over rapidly boiling water.
Steam 6-8 minutes, until the strings look glossy and set and no longer taste of raw flour.
steps.tip: Over-steaming makes them gummy. Six minutes is usually enough for a single layer.

steps.text: Lift off and let them cool for 2 minutes before easing them off the plate, or they will tear.

recipes.storage: Best within a few hours. Keeps 2 days refrigerated in a covered box; re-steam 3 minutes to bring the softness back — reheating dry turns them to string.

recipes.name: Kadala Curry
recipes.subtitle: black chickpeas in dark roasted coconut gravy, the breakfast partner to puttu

ingredients.note: black chickpeas, kadala
for roasting and grinding

prepNotes: Soak the black chickpeas at least 8 hours or overnight. They are much harder than white chana and will not soften otherwise.
The colour and depth of this curry come from roasting the coconut almost to the point of burning. Do it first, while the chickpeas cook.
Grind the roasted coconut with 1/2 cup water to as smooth a paste as your blender will manage — this gravy should not be gritty.

steps.text: Pressure cook the soaked chickpeas with 3 cups water, the turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 5 whistles, then 10 minutes on low. Release naturally and keep the cooking liquid.
steps.tip: The cooking water is dark and flavourful. Never throw it away — it is the base of the gravy.

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp coconut oil in a heavy pan and fry the sliced shallots for 4 minutes until browning at the edges.
Add the grated coconut and roast on medium-low, stirring constantly, for 10-12 minutes until it is a deep chocolate brown.
steps.tip: Ten minutes feels long and the last two are where it happens. Do not walk away.

steps.text: Add the coriander powder, chilli powder and fennel seeds and roast 1 minute more, until the spices darken and smell toasted.
Cool slightly, then blend with 1/2 cup water to a fine dark paste.

In the same pan heat the remaining 2 tbsp oil, pop the mustard seeds, then add the broken red chillies, curry leaves, chopped onion, ginger and garlic. Cook 6 minutes until the onion is soft and gold.
Stir in the ground coconut paste and fry 4 minutes until the oil begins to separate at the edges.
Add the cooked chickpeas with their liquid and the garam masala. Simmer uncovered 12-15 minutes until the gravy thickens enough to coat a spoon.
steps.tip: Mash a spoonful of the chickpeas against the side of the pan to thicken the gravy naturally.

steps.text: Taste for salt and rest 10 minutes off the heat before serving with puttu or appam.

recipes.storage: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and freezes well for a month. It thickens overnight; reheat with a splash of water over medium heat until it loosens.

recipes.name: Kerala Meen Curry
recipes.subtitle: Fish simmered in coconut milk and kokum, tempered with curry leaves and coconut oil

ingredients.note: kingfish, seer, pomfret or any firm white fish
kudampuli / gambooge; soak in warm water 10 min
or 1 small onion

prepNotes: Kokum (locally kudampuli) is the defining sour note. Tamarind will work but gives a rounder, sweeter sourness and a different colour.
Never boil a coconut milk curry hard after the thick milk goes in; it will split. Keep it at a bare tremble.
Traditionally cooked in a clay meen chatti, which holds heat gently. A heavy pan is fine.

steps.text: Heat the coconut oil. Splutter the mustard seeds and fenugreek, then add the curry leaves, shallots, ginger, garlic and green chillies. Fry until the shallots soften and turn pale gold.
Lower the heat, add the turmeric and Kashmiri chilli and stir for 30 seconds only. Powdered chilli scorches fast and turns bitter.
Add the soaked kokum with its water, the thin part of the coconut milk and salt. Simmer 8 minutes to build the base.
Slide in the fish in a single layer. Do not stir; shake the pan instead so the pieces stay whole. Simmer 6-8 minutes until just opaque.
Pour in the thick coconut milk, swirl the pan and heat through without letting it boil. Take it off the heat as soon as it steams.
steps.tip: Finish with a teaspoon of raw coconut oil and a fresh sprig of curry leaves.

steps.text: Rest at least an hour before eating. This curry is markedly better after resting, and better still the next day.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated and genuinely improves overnight. Do not freeze; the fish turns woolly and the coconut milk separates. Reheat gently without boiling.

recipes.name: Meen Varuthathu
recipes.subtitle: chilli-and-pepper crusted fish shallow fried in coconut oil until the edges blister

ingredients.qty: 600g, 4 steaks or whole small fish, slashed
ingredients.note: seer, pomfret or mackerel
for colour without ferocious heat
for the crust

prepNotes: Pat the fish bone dry with paper towel and cut two deep slashes into each side, right down to the bone. Wet fish will never crisp.
Mix the chilli powders, turmeric, pepper, ginger, garlic, lemon juice and salt into a thick paste with 1 tbsp water and rub it into the slashes.
Marinate 30 minutes at room temperature, or up to 2 hours refrigerated. Longer than that and the lemon starts to cook the flesh.

steps.text: Bring the marinated fish back to room temperature for 15 minutes if it has been in the fridge.
Dust each piece lightly with rice flour on both sides and shake off the excess.
steps.tip: A thin film only. A thick coat turns pasty in the pan.

steps.text: Heat the coconut oil in a heavy tawa over medium-high until a pinch of flour dropped in sizzles instantly.
Slide in the fish, laying it away from you, and do not touch it for 4 minutes.
steps.tip: Moving it early tears the crust off. Wait until it releases on its own.

steps.text: Turn once and fry the second side 3-4 minutes until the crust is deep brick red and the flesh at the slash is opaque.
Throw the curry leaves into the hot oil around the fish for the last 30 seconds until they crisp.
steps.tip: Stand back — wet leaves in hot oil spit hard.

steps.text: Lift onto a plate, scatter the crisped leaves over, and serve within minutes with rice and a wedge of lemon.

recipes.storage: Eat hot from the pan. Leftovers keep 1 day refrigerated; re-crisp in a dry hot pan for 2 minutes a side rather than reheating in a microwave.

recipes.name: Mutta Roast
recipes.subtitle: boiled eggs in a dark slow-fried onion masala, breakfast alongside appam

ingredients.note: the volume looks absurd and then it collapses
for colour

prepNotes: Boil the eggs 9 minutes from a rolling boil, then cool them in cold water before peeling — the yolks stay just set and the shells slip off.
Slice the onions as thin as you can manage. Thin slices melt into the masala; thick ones stay as visible strands.
Score each peeled egg with 3 shallow slits so the masala gets inside rather than sliding off.

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp coconut oil in a kadhai and fry the scored eggs with a pinch of turmeric and salt for 2 minutes, turning, until blistered and gold. Lift out.
steps.tip: Keep a lid handy — eggs spit in hot oil.

steps.text: Add the remaining oil, then the sliced onions, ginger, garlic, green chillies and 2 sprigs of curry leaves with a pinch of salt.
Cook on medium-low for 20-25 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until the onions collapse to about a fifth of their volume and turn a deep glossy brown.
steps.tip: This is the entire dish and there is no shortcut. Twenty-five minutes, low and slow.

steps.text: Add the chilli powder, Kashmiri chilli, coriander powder, turmeric and pepper. Fry 90 seconds with a splash of water so the spices do not catch.
Stir in the tomatoes and cook 8 minutes until they break down completely and the oil pools at the edges.
steps.tip: Wait for the oil to separate. That is the signal the masala is cooked, not merely hot.

steps.text: Add 1/4 cup water, the garam masala and fennel powder, and simmer 3 minutes into a thick clinging masala.
Return the fried eggs, roll them in the masala and cook 3 minutes on low so they take on the colour.
Scatter over the last sprig of curry leaves, cover and rest 5 minutes off the heat before serving with appam or bread.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated; the masala improves but the whites toughen a little. Reheat over low heat with 2 tbsp water, turning the eggs gently.

recipes.name: Nadan Chicken Stew
recipes.subtitle: pale peppery chicken and potato stew in coconut milk, the classic appam partner

ingredients.note: the only heat that belongs here
400ml thin, 100ml thick

prepNotes: Stew is a white curry: no turmeric, no chilli powder, no browning. Keep the heat low the whole way through.
Separate your coconut milk before you start — thin for cooking, thick for finishing. If using tinned, dilute 150ml with 250ml water for the thin.
Cut the potato into chunks no smaller than 4cm so they hold their shape through 25 minutes of simmering.

steps.text: Heat the coconut oil in a heavy pot over medium-low and add the cinnamon, cloves and cardamom. Fry 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the onion, ginger, garlic and green chillies with a pinch of salt. Cook 6-8 minutes until soft and glassy.
steps.tip: Do not let them colour. Any browning and it stops being a stew.

steps.text: Stir in the crushed pepper and fry 30 seconds.
Add the chicken and turn it in the aromatics for 3 minutes until the flesh turns opaque white.
Pour in the thin coconut milk, add the potato, carrot, curry leaves and salt, and bring to a bare simmer.
Cover and cook on low for 25 minutes, until the chicken pulls easily from the bone and the potato is soft at the centre.
steps.tip: A hard boil will curdle the coconut milk and toughen the chicken. Keep it at a lazy blip.

steps.text: Uncover and stir in the thick coconut milk. Warm through for 2 minutes without letting it boil.
Taste for salt and pepper, then rest covered for 10 minutes off the heat before serving with appam.
steps.tip: The stew tastes noticeably better after ten minutes of sitting. Build it into your timing.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated and improves overnight. Reheat over low heat, stirring, and add a splash of water — it thickens considerably when cold.

recipes.name: Olan
recipes.subtitle: ash gourd and cowpeas simmered in thin coconut milk, barely spiced on purpose

ingredients.qty: 400g, peeled and cut into 4cm thin slices

ingredients.note: red cowpeas (van payar) are traditional
300ml thin, 100ml thick — see prep notes
raw, stirred in at the end

prepNotes: Soak the cowpeas 6 hours or overnight. They stay firm otherwise and will not cook alongside the gourd.
If you are using tinned coconut milk, dilute 100ml with 200ml water to stand in for the second and third pressings, and keep 100ml undiluted for the finish.
Olan carries no onion, garlic, mustard or chilli powder. The restraint is the dish — resist adding any.

steps.text: Boil the soaked cowpeas in 2 cups of water for 20-25 minutes until soft but still holding their shape. Drain, keeping a little of the cooking water.
steps.tip: Squeeze one between your fingers — it should give completely with no chalky centre.

steps.text: Put the ash gourd slices in a wide pan with the slit chillies, salt and just enough water to come halfway up.
Simmer uncovered 8 minutes until the gourd turns translucent at the edges and a knife slides through without resistance.
steps.tip: Ash gourd goes from firm to mush in about two minutes. Check early.

steps.text: Add the cooked cowpeas and the thin coconut milk. Bring to a bare simmer.
Cook 5 minutes on low, shaking the pan rather than stirring so the gourd slices stay whole.
Pour in the thick coconut milk and the curry leaves. Warm through for 1 minute only.
steps.tip: Do not let it boil after the thick milk goes in or it will split into oily flecks.

steps.text: Take off the heat, stir in the raw coconut oil and cover for 5 minutes before serving.
steps.tip: The raw oil is the signature aroma of olan. Use good unrefined coconut oil.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat very gently over low heat without boiling; it will thicken as it sits, so loosen with a spoonful of water.

recipes.name: Parippu Curry
recipes.subtitle: soft moong dal in coconut and cumin, the first course of a sadya

ingredients.note: cherupayar parippu
goes into the paste

prepNotes: Dry-roast the moong dal in a pan for 4-5 minutes until it smells nutty and a few grains turn pale gold. This is what separates parippu curry from ordinary dal.
Rinse the roasted dal in two changes of water before cooking.
Grind the coconut, green chillies, cumin and garlic to a fine paste with 1/3 cup water while the dal cooks.

steps.text: Pressure cook the rinsed dal with 2.5 cups water and the turmeric for 3 whistles, then rest until the pressure drops.
steps.tip: It should be completely collapsed. Undercooked parippu curry has a raw beany edge that no amount of coconut hides.

steps.text: Whisk the cooked dal smooth with a ladle, adding hot water until it is the consistency of thin cream.
Stir in the ground coconut paste and the salt.
Simmer on low for 6-8 minutes, stirring often, until the raw coconut smell disappears and it thickens slightly.
steps.tip: Coconut catches on the base easily. Stir and keep the flame low.

steps.text: Heat the coconut oil in a small pan and pop the mustard seeds, about 30 seconds.
Add the sliced shallots, broken red chillies and curry leaves and fry 2 minutes until the shallots brown.
Pour the tempering over the dal and cover for 5 minutes so the curry leaf aroma settles in.
Serve over hot rice as the first course of the meal, with a papadam crushed over the top.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. It sets almost solid when cold — reheat with plenty of hot water, whisking, until it pours again.

recipes.name: Pazham Pori
recipes.subtitle: ripe plantain slices in a turmeric-gold batter, the four o'clock teashop snack

ingredients.note: use ripe nendran plantains — catalogued here as raw-banana
for crispness
for the classic yellow
or neutral oil

prepNotes: The plantains must be properly ripe — skin heavily blackened, flesh soft and sweet. Underripe nendran is starchy and the snack falls flat.
Make the batter 10 minutes ahead and let it rest so the flour hydrates; it will cling better to the slippery banana.
The batter should be the thickness of pouring cream: thick enough to coat the back of a spoon, thin enough to drip off in a steady ribbon.

steps.text: Whisk the maida, rice flour, turmeric, sugar, salt and crushed cumin together in a bowl.
Add the water gradually, whisking, until you have a smooth lump-free batter. Rest 10 minutes.
steps.tip: Add the last of the water a tablespoon at a time — flours vary and a thin batter slides straight off.

steps.text: Peel the plantains and slice each lengthwise into 3-4 flat strips about 8mm thick.
steps.tip: Too thin and they disintegrate in the oil; too thick and the centre stays firm.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a kadhai to 175C — a drop of batter should rise and sizzle within 3 seconds without browning instantly.
Dip a strip into the batter, let the excess run off, and lower it gently into the oil.
Fry 3-4 at a time for 2 minutes, until the underside is set and pale gold.
steps.tip: Crowding the pan drops the oil temperature and the fritters drink oil instead of frying.

steps.text: Turn and fry a further 2 minutes until both sides are deep gold and the surface has stopped bubbling hard.
Lift onto a rack, not paper, so the underside stays crisp. Repeat with the rest.
Serve hot with strong black tea.

recipes.storage: Eat within an hour — they soften as they sit. Leftovers can be crisped in a hot oven for 5 minutes, but they will never be as good as the first batch.

recipes.name: Pulissery
recipes.subtitle: soured yogurt and coconut curry, gently spiced and never boiled

ingredients.note: a day-old yogurt is ideal
or raw banana, cut the same way
whole seeds, not dried leaves

prepNotes: Take the yogurt out of the fridge 30 minutes ahead. Cold yogurt hitting a hot pan splits immediately.
Whisk the yogurt completely smooth with 1/2 cup water before it goes anywhere near heat — any lump will curdle.
Grind the coconut, green chillies, cumin and turmeric to a fine paste with 4 tbsp water. Fine matters: a gritty paste makes a gritty curry.

steps.text: Cook the ash gourd with the salt and 1/2 cup water in a wide pan, covered, for 8 minutes until soft and translucent.
Stir in the ground coconut paste and simmer 4 minutes on low, until the raw coconut smell has gone.
Take the pan off the heat completely and let it cool for 3 minutes.
steps.tip: This pause is what keeps the yogurt from splitting. Do not skip it.

steps.text: Pour in the whisked yogurt, stirring as you go.
Return to the lowest possible heat and warm, stirring constantly, for 3-4 minutes until it just steams and thickens slightly.
steps.tip: The instant you see a bubble, pull it off. Boiled pulissery separates and cannot be rescued.

steps.text: Taste for salt and set aside covered.
Heat the coconut oil in a small pan, pop the mustard seeds, then add the fenugreek seeds, broken red chillies and curry leaves and fry 20 seconds.
steps.tip: Fenugreek burns bitter fast. It should darken only a shade.

steps.text: Pour the tempering over the curry and cover for 5 minutes before serving with rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated and the sourness deepens. Reheat only to lukewarm over the lowest heat, or serve at room temperature as they do in Kerala.

recipes.name: Pumpkin Erissery
recipes.subtitle: mashed pumpkin and cowpeas under a lid of dark roasted coconut

ingredients.note: red cowpeas
half for the paste, half for the roast

prepNotes: Soak the cowpeas overnight, or at least 6 hours. Unsoaked they take twice as long as the pumpkin and the dish falls apart waiting for them.
Grind half the grated coconut with the green chillies, garlic, half the cumin and the turmeric to a smooth paste with 3 tbsp water.
Keep the other half of the coconut dry and loose for roasting — it must not be damp or it will steam rather than brown.

steps.text: Boil the soaked cowpeas in 2 cups water for 20 minutes until tender. Do not drain.
Add the pumpkin cubes, chilli powder and salt to the same pan with a little more water if needed. Cook covered 10 minutes until the pumpkin is soft enough to crush against the side of the pan.
Mash roughly with the back of a ladle, leaving some cubes whole for texture.
steps.tip: Erissery is a mash, not a puree. Stop while you can still see pieces.

steps.text: Stir in the ground coconut paste and simmer 5 minutes on low until it loses its raw smell and thickens.
In a separate kadhai, heat the coconut oil and pop the mustard seeds, about 30 seconds.
Add the broken red chillies, curry leaves and the remaining cumin seeds and fry 20 seconds.
Add the reserved grated coconut and roast on medium-low, stirring constantly, for 5-6 minutes until it is a deep even brown and smells nutty.
steps.tip: This is the whole point of erissery and it turns from brown to burnt in seconds. Stand over it.

steps.text: Pour the roasted coconut tempering over the pumpkin, stir once, and rest 5 minutes before serving.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. Reheat gently with a splash of water; the roasted coconut aroma fades, so a fresh spoonful of the tempering revives it.

recipes.name: Puttu
recipes.subtitle: steamed cylinders of rice flour layered with coconut, eaten hot with kadala curry

ingredients.note: coarse puttu podi if available
added a sprinkle at a time

prepNotes: If your rice flour is not pre-roasted, dry-roast it in a pan on low for 6-8 minutes until it smells toasty and feels warm but takes no colour. Cool completely before wetting it.
The moisture level is everything. The flour is right when a fistful holds its shape when squeezed but crumbles apart cleanly when you poke it.
Rest the wetted flour 10 minutes before steaming so the water distributes evenly.

steps.text: Dissolve the salt in the warm water.
Sprinkle the salted water over the rice flour a tablespoon at a time, rubbing it through with your fingertips after each addition.
steps.tip: Never pour. Poured water makes lumps that steam into hard pellets.

steps.text: Stop when the flour feels like damp sand and holds a shape in your fist. You may not need all the water.
Pass the whole lot through a coarse sieve or break the lumps by rubbing between your palms, then rest 10 minutes.
Bring water to a rolling boil in the base of the puttu maker or steamer.
Load the mould: a tablespoon of grated coconut at the bottom, then loose flour to two-thirds, then coconut, then flour, finishing with coconut. Do not press down.
steps.tip: Packing the flour is the classic mistake. Loose layers steam through; packed ones come out dense.

steps.text: Steam 7-8 minutes from when a steady plume comes out of the top.
Push the puttu out onto a plate with the handle of a wooden spoon and serve immediately with kadala curry or ripe banana.
steps.tip: Puttu hardens as it cools. Steam it in batches and eat each one as it comes.

recipes.storage: Eat straight from the steamer. Leftovers harden within an hour; crumble them and re-steam 3 minutes, or fry the crumbs with coconut, jaggery and cardamom the next morning.

recipes.name: Amti
recipes.subtitle: toor dal made sweet, sour and dark with goda masala, tamarind and jaggery

ingredients.note: stand-in for goda masala; use goda masala if you can get it
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Rinse and soak the dal 20 minutes so it cooks to a uniform mush.
Soak the tamarind in 3 tbsp hot water for 15 minutes and squeeze out the pulp, or use a ready thick pulp.
Amti wants a balance of sweet, sour and hot — taste and adjust jaggery and tamarind at the end, not the beginning.

steps.text: Pressure cook the soaked dal with the turmeric and 300ml water for 4 whistles until completely soft, then whisk it smooth.
Heat the oil in a pan, pop the mustard seeds, then add the cumin, curry leaves and hing and let them sizzle 10 seconds.
steps.tip: Wait for the mustard seeds to actually pop. Adding the rest too early gives you raw mustard in the finished dal.

steps.text: Add the kashmiri chilli and chilli powder and stir for 10 seconds off the heat so they bloom without burning.
Pour in the whisked dal and the remaining 200ml water and bring to a simmer.
Stir in the goda masala, tamarind pulp, jaggery and salt.
Simmer uncovered 12 minutes, stirring now and then, until the amti darkens and thins slightly and a skin no longer forms on top.
steps.tip: It should be pourable, not thick — amti is drunk as much as eaten.

steps.text: Taste and adjust: more jaggery if it bites, more tamarind if it tastes flat.
Finish with the grated coconut and coriander and serve with rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and tastes better on day two. Reheat gently with a splash of water; do not boil hard or the coconut splits out.

recipes.name: Batata Bhaji
recipes.subtitle: soft turmeric-yellow potatoes with mustard seeds, curry leaves and green chilli

ingredients.qty: 500g, boiled, peeled and roughly broken by hand

ingredients.note: use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Boil the potatoes the night before if you can — cold boiled potato breaks into rough chunks instead of turning to mash.
Break the potatoes by hand rather than cutting them; the ragged edges hold the tempering.

steps.text: Boil the potatoes whole in their skins until a knife goes through easily, about 20 minutes, then cool, peel and break into rough 3cm pieces.
steps.tip: Cook them whole and unpeeled or they take on water and go slimy.

steps.text: Heat the oil and pop the mustard seeds, then add the cumin, curry leaves and hing.
Add the green chilli and sliced onion and cook 5 minutes until the onion is soft and translucent.
Stir in the turmeric and let it cook 20 seconds in the oil.
Add the potato, salt and sugar and turn everything over gently until the pieces are evenly yellow.
steps.tip: Fold with a flat spatula from underneath. Stirring turns this into mashed potato.

steps.text: Pour in the water, cover and steam on low heat for 5 minutes.
Squeeze over the lemon, fold through the coriander and serve with pooris, chapati or as the filling for vada pav.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat covered over low heat with 2 tbsp water; it also makes the best possible sandwich filling cold.

recipes.name: Bharli Vangi
recipes.subtitle: baby aubergines stuffed with roasted peanut, coconut and goda masala, simmered in their own gravy

ingredients.qty: 500g small round aubergines (about 8), stems left on

ingredients.note: khobra; the roasting is what makes the masala dark

ingredients.qty: 2 medium, 1 chopped for the masala and 1 for the gravy

ingredients.note: stand-in for goda masala; use goda masala if you can get it

prepNotes: Slit the aubergines into a cross from the base, stopping 1cm short of the stem, and drop them into salted water while you make the masala.
Roast the peanut, dried coconut and sesame separately — they brown at completely different speeds.
Soak the tamarind in 3 tbsp hot water for 15 minutes and squeeze out the pulp.

steps.text: Dry-roast the grated dried coconut over low heat for 4 minutes until it is a deep golden brown, then tip it straight out of the pan.
steps.tip: It goes from golden to burnt in about fifteen seconds. Do not walk away.

steps.text: Grind the roasted coconut, peanut and sesame with one chopped onion, the garlic and the ginger to a coarse, thick masala using 3 tbsp water.
Mix the masala with the goda masala, coriander powder, chilli powder, turmeric, half the tamarind pulp, the jaggery and salt.
Drain the aubergines, pat dry and pack about a tablespoon of masala into each slit, keeping the fruit whole. Reserve the leftover masala.
steps.tip: Stuff them full but do not force the slits open — a split aubergine falls apart in the pan.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a wide pan and lay the stuffed aubergines in a single layer. Fry 6 minutes, turning them by shaking the pan, until the skins blister and dull.
Lift the aubergines out, add the second onion, sliced, and cook 5 minutes until soft.
Stir in the reserved masala and fry 4 minutes until it darkens and oil separates at the edges.
Add the water and the remaining tamarind, return the aubergines to the pan, cover and simmer 20 minutes over low heat.
steps.tip: Turn them by shaking the pan, never with a spoon. They are soft and will collapse.

steps.text: Check that a knife slides into an aubergine without resistance, and that the gravy is thick and rust-coloured with oil floating on top.
Scatter with coriander and rest 10 minutes before serving with bhakri or rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and improves overnight. Reheat covered over low heat with 3 tbsp water, shaking rather than stirring.

recipes.name: Jowar Bhakri
recipes.subtitle: an unleavened sorghum flatbread patted out by hand, nutty and slightly coarse

ingredients.note: fresh flour; old jowar flour will not bind
for dusting, if the dough sticks

prepNotes: Jowar has no gluten, so the dough is bound by hot water and kneading alone. The water must be at a rolling boil, not merely hot.
Clear a patch of clean, dry counter — bhakri is patted out flat on the surface, not rolled with a pin.
Get the tawa heating before you shape the first one. A cold tawa gives you a leathery bhakri.

steps.text: Bring the water to a rolling boil with the salt.
Put the flour in a wide bowl and pour in about three quarters of the boiling water, mixing with the handle of a wooden spoon until it comes together in a shaggy mass.
steps.tip: Add the rest of the water a splash at a time. Different flours drink different amounts.

steps.text: As soon as it is cool enough to touch, knead firmly for 5 minutes with the heel of your hand until the dough is smooth and shows no cracks when you press it.
steps.tip: Knead it while it is still hot. Once it cools it will never bind, and every bhakri will crack at the edge.

steps.text: Divide into 6 balls and keep them covered with a damp cloth.
Dust the counter with jowar flour, flatten a ball with your palm, then pat it out into a 15cm disc by pressing and rotating with the flat of your fingers.
steps.tip: Work from the centre outwards and turn the disc a quarter every few pats, so it stays round and even.

steps.text: Brush the loose flour off, lift the bhakri on your palm and lay it onto the hot tawa.
Smear the top surface with water using your fingers and cook 1 minute, until the wet film dries and the underside shows pale brown patches.
Flip and cook the second side 1 minute, then flip once more and press around the edges with a folded cloth until it puffs up like a balloon.
steps.tip: If it will not puff, the dough was too dry or the tawa too cool. It will still taste right.

steps.text: Stack the finished bhakris in a cloth-lined basket and serve hot with zunka, pithla or usal.

recipes.storage: Bhakri is best within the hour. It keeps 1 day wrapped in a cloth and stiffens as it cools; revive on a dry tawa for 30 seconds a side with a flick of water.

recipes.name: Kanda Poha
recipes.subtitle: flattened rice steamed soft with onion, peanuts and curry leaves, breakfast in fifteen minutes

ingredients.note: thin poha turns to paste; buy the thick jada poha
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
Maharashtrian poha is faintly sweet
makes it kanda-batata poha

prepNotes: Rinse the poha in a colander under running water, tossing with your fingers, then leave it to stand 10 minutes. Never soak it in a bowl of water.
Chop the onion fine and have everything within reach — once the mustard seeds pop the dish takes six minutes.

steps.text: Rinse the poha in a colander until the grains soften, then leave it to drain and swell for 10 minutes.
steps.tip: Squeeze one grain: it should crush cleanly. Hard in the middle means another sprinkle of water; mushy means you soaked it.

steps.text: Toss the drained poha with the turmeric, sugar and salt so every grain turns yellow. Do this with your fingertips, not a spoon.
Fry the peanuts in the oil over medium heat for 3 minutes until they darken and smell toasted, then lift them out.
Into the same oil add the mustard seeds and wait for them to pop, then the cumin, green chilli, curry leaves and hing.
steps.tip: Stand back — wet curry leaves spit.

steps.text: Add the diced potato, if using, cover and cook 6 minutes until tender.
Add the onion and cook 4 minutes until soft and translucent but not browned.
steps.tip: Browned onion makes the poha taste of fried onion instead of fresh.

steps.text: Fold in the poha and the fried peanuts, lower the heat, cover and steam 3 minutes.
Turn off the heat, squeeze over the lemon and scatter with coriander and grated coconut. Serve at once.

recipes.storage: Poha is a fifteen-minute dish and does not keep — it dries out within a couple of hours. If you must, refrigerate 1 day and revive it with a sprinkle of water, covered, over low heat.

recipes.name: Kolhapuri Chicken Rassa
recipes.subtitle: thin, fiery red chicken curry built on roasted coconut and dagad phool

ingredients.qty: 800g, on the bone, cut into curry pieces
3 medium, 2 for the masala and 1 for the gravy

ingredients.note: khobra; roasted almost black, this is the backbone of kala masala
for the red without wrecking anyone
Kolhapur would use more
dagad phool; the smoky note that makes this taste Kolhapuri

prepNotes: Marinate the chicken with the turmeric, half the ginger-garlic and 1 tsp salt for 30 minutes at room temperature.
Roast the whole spices, the dried coconut and the sesame separately, then cool them completely before grinding — warm spices grind into a paste that turns bitter.
The rassa is meant to be thin and drinkable. Keep 600ml water to hand and do not let it reduce to a thick gravy.

steps.text: Grind the ginger and garlic to a paste and rub half of it into the chicken with the turmeric and salt. Leave 30 minutes.
Dry-roast the grated dried coconut over low heat for 5 minutes until it is dark brown and smells toasted, then tip it out immediately.
steps.tip: Dark brown, not black. Burnt coconut makes the whole pot bitter and there is no fixing it.

steps.text: In the same pan, dry-roast the cumin, black pepper, cloves, cinnamon, black cardamom, stone flower, poppy seeds and sesame for 2 minutes until fragrant. Cool completely.
Fry 2 sliced onions in 2 tbsp of the oil over medium heat for 10 minutes until deep brown, then cool.
Grind the roasted coconut, roasted spices, fried onion, kashmiri chilli, chilli powder and coriander powder with 100ml water to a smooth dark masala.
Heat the remaining oil in a heavy pan with the bay leaf, add the last onion, finely chopped, and cook 8 minutes until golden.
Add the remaining ginger-garlic paste, fry 1 minute, then add the chicken and sear over high heat for 5 minutes until the pieces are opaque all over.
Stir in the ground masala and fry over medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes, scraping the base, until it darkens and oil pools at the sides.
steps.tip: This is the step that decides the curry. Under-fried masala tastes raw and grainy no matter how long you simmer it afterwards.

steps.text: Pour in the water, season with salt, bring to a boil then simmer uncovered 25 minutes until the chicken is tender and a red film of oil floats on the surface.
Stir in the fresh coconut, if using, check the salt and finish with coriander.
Rest 10 minutes off the heat and serve with bhakri or chapati and raw onion.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and is better the next day. Reheat over low heat with a splash of water; it also freezes well for 2 months.

recipes.name: Matki Usal
recipes.subtitle: sprouted moth beans in a thin dark gravy of onion, roasted coconut and goda masala

ingredients.note: stand-in for goda or kala masala; use either if you have it
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
