prepNotes: Sprouting matki takes two days: soak the beans 8 hours, drain, tie them in a damp cloth and leave in a warm place 24 to 36 hours until the tails are about 5mm.
Dry-roast the grated dried coconut until deep brown and grind it with the onion, garlic and ginger before you light the pan.
Rinse the sprouts and pick out any that have not opened.

steps.text: Grind the roasted dried coconut with half the onion, the garlic and the ginger to a coarse paste with 3 tbsp water.
Heat the oil, pop the mustard seeds, then add the cumin, curry leaves and hing.
Add the remaining chopped onion and cook 6 minutes until golden at the edges.
Stir in the coconut paste and fry 5 minutes over medium heat until it darkens and stops smelling raw.
steps.tip: Keep scraping the base — coconut paste catches fast.

steps.text: Add the chilli powder, kashmiri chilli, coriander powder, turmeric and goda masala and fry 1 minute.
Tip in the sprouts, turn them through the masala and cook 3 minutes.
Add the water, salt, jaggery and tamarind, bring to a boil, then cover and simmer 18 minutes until the beans are soft but still hold their shape.
steps.tip: Pressure cooking is faster but turns them to mush. Eighteen minutes open is worth the time.

steps.text: Uncover and check the gravy: it should be thin, dark and slick with red oil on top. Loosen with hot water if it has tightened.
Finish with coriander and serve with bhakri, or with pav and chopped onion.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and thickens as the beans drink the gravy; loosen with hot water when reheating. Freezes 1 month.

recipes.name: Misal Pav
recipes.subtitle: Sprouted beans under a fiery kat, topped with farsan and eaten with pav

ingredients.note: Kolhapuri if you have it
goda masala traditionally

prepNotes: Misal is two things in one bowl: the usal, a mild sprouted-bean curry, and the kat, the fiery red oil-slicked gravy poured over it. Make them separately.
The floating layer of red oil on top is the signature. Do not stir it in or skim it off.

steps.text: Pressure cook the sprouts with turmeric and salt until just tender, 2 whistles. They should hold their shape.
For the kat masala, dry roast the coconut, peanut and sesame until deep brown, then blend with two onions, tomato, garlic and ginger to a paste.
steps.tip: Take the coconut properly dark — that is where the colour and depth come from.

steps.text: Heat oil, splutter the mustard seeds and curry leaves, add the remaining chopped onion, then the ground paste. Fry until the oil separates.
Add the chilli powder, coriander, cumin and garam masala and cook a further 2 minutes.
Add 3 cups of hot water and simmer 15 minutes. The kat should be thin and carry a visible layer of red oil.
To serve, spoon the usal into bowls, ladle the kat over, and top with farsan, raw onion, coriander and lemon. Pav alongside.

recipes.storage: Usal and kat both keep 3 days refrigerated and are better on day two. Assemble only at the moment of serving or the farsan goes soft.

recipes.name: Pav Bhaji
recipes.subtitle: mashed vegetables cooked down red and buttery, eaten with griddled pav

image.alt: Pav bhaji with buttered pav, chopped onion and lemon

ingredients.note: fresh or frozen

ingredients.qty: 2 medium, finely chopped, plus 1 raw for serving

ingredients.note: colour without the burn
for heat, to taste
stand-in for pav bhaji masala; use ready pav bhaji masala if you have it
half into the bhaji, half for the pav

prepNotes: Boil the potato, cauliflower and peas together beforehand — they should be soft enough to mash with a spoon.
Chop the tomatoes as fine as you can; they have to melt, not sit in pieces.
Weigh the butter out and keep it cold. Pav bhaji is not the place to guess.

steps.text: Boil the potato, cauliflower and peas in salted water until completely soft, about 15 minutes, then drain and keep the pan warm.
steps.tip: Undercooked cauliflower stays stringy and no amount of mashing will fix it later.

steps.text: Melt 40g of the butter on a large tawa or wide pan and cook the chopped onion over medium heat until soft and translucent, about 6 minutes.
Add the garlic and ginger and fry 1 minute, until the raw edge disappears.
Stir in the capsicum and cook 3 minutes, just until it loses its squeak.
Add the tomato and cook down for 10 minutes, pressing it against the pan, until the mass darkens and oil beads at the edges.
steps.tip: This is the step everyone shortens. If the tomato still smells sharp, keep going.

steps.text: Add the kashmiri chilli, garam masala, coriander powder, cumin powder, turmeric, amchur and chilli powder and fry 1 minute.
Tip in the drained vegetables and mash them straight into the pan with a potato masher until no lumps remain.
Pour in the water, season with salt, and simmer 10 minutes, mashing and stirring, until the bhaji is thick and glossy and a spoon leaves a trail.
Stir 20g of butter through the bhaji off the heat and scatter with coriander.
Split the pav, griddle them cut side down in the remaining butter with a pinch of the masala until the edges are crisp and red, about 2 minutes.
steps.tip: Griddle the pav only when everyone is at the table — they go leathery within minutes.

steps.text: Serve the bhaji with the hot pav, raw chopped onion and lemon wedges.

recipes.storage: The bhaji keeps 3 days refrigerated and thickens as it sits; reheat with a splash of water and a fresh knob of butter. Griddle the pav to order.

recipes.name: Pithla
recipes.subtitle: loose gram flour curry slackened with sour buttermilk, garlicky and made in ten minutes

ingredients.note: the sourness is the point; leave fresh buttermilk out overnight
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Whisk the besan into the cold buttermilk before anything goes on the heat. Lumps formed in a hot pan never come out.
Sour buttermilk gives pithla its character — leave fresh buttermilk on the counter overnight, or stir a squeeze of lemon into it.
Have the bhakri dough ready if you are eating it the proper way; pithla waits for nobody.

steps.text: Whisk the besan into the cold buttermilk with the turmeric and salt until completely smooth, then whisk in the water.
steps.tip: Push the slurry through a sieve if you see any lumps. Thirty seconds now saves the dish.

steps.text: Heat the oil, pop the mustard seeds, then add the cumin, curry leaves and hing.
Add the garlic and green chilli and fry 1 minute until the garlic smells sweet but has not coloured.
Add the onion, if using, and cook 4 minutes until soft.
Pour in the besan slurry in a slow stream, stirring continuously.
Bring to a gentle boil and simmer 8 to 10 minutes, stirring often, until it thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon and the raw besan smell is gone.
steps.tip: It thickens a lot as it cools, so pull it off looser than you want to serve it.

steps.text: Check the salt, fold through the coriander and pour into bowls.
Serve immediately with hot jowar bhakri, raw onion and a green chilli.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated but sets firm. Reheat over low heat with 3 to 4 tbsp water, whisking, until it loosens back to a pouring consistency.

recipes.name: Puran Poli
recipes.subtitle: a soft flatbread stuffed with sweet chana dal and jaggery, scented with cardamom and nutmeg

ingredients.note: use the dark, soft variety
keeps the covering stretchy enough to hold the puran
for the colour of the dough
2 in the dough, the rest for cooking and serving
for dusting

ingredients.qty: about 100ml for the dough, 500ml for the dal

prepNotes: Make the dough first and rest it at least 1 hour, covered, under a film of ghee. A slack, well-rested dough is the whole trick.
Rinse and soak the chana dal 2 hours before cooking so it cooks evenly and does not need extra water at the end.
Have a colander ready to drain the cooked dal thoroughly — wet puran will never hold inside the poli.

steps.text: Knead the atta, maida, turmeric, salt, 2 tbsp ghee and enough water into a very soft, sticky dough, working it for 8 minutes until it stretches without tearing.
steps.tip: It should be softer than chapati dough, almost too soft to handle. That is correct.

steps.text: Coat the dough with a spoon of ghee, cover and rest at least 1 hour.
Pressure cook the soaked chana dal with 500ml water for 4 whistles until soft but not disintegrating, then drain it thoroughly in a colander for 10 minutes.
steps.tip: Keep the drained cooking water — thinned with spices it becomes katachi amti, which is served alongside.

steps.text: Mash or pass the drained dal through a sieve until completely smooth.

Cook the mashed dal with the jaggery in a heavy pan over medium heat for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring constantly, until the mixture pulls away from the sides and holds a line when you drag a spoon through it.
steps.tip: Jaggery loosens the mix before it tightens. Do not panic and do not stop stirring, or it catches.

steps.text: Stir in the cardamom and nutmeg and let the puran cool completely — it should be firm enough to roll into balls.
Divide both dough and puran into 8 portions each, with the puran balls slightly larger than the dough balls.
Flatten a dough ball in your palm, sit a puran ball in the middle, gather the edges over the top and pinch them shut, then flatten gently.
Dust with rice flour and roll out very gently to about 18cm, turning often and using almost no pressure.
steps.tip: If the filling breaks through, patch it with a scrap of dough and carry on rolling from the centre outwards.

steps.text: Cook on a medium-hot tawa for about 1 minute a side until pale brown spots appear, smearing each side with ghee as you turn it.
Serve warm with a spoon of ghee poured over, and katachi amti alongside.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days at room temperature in an airtight box, or 1 week refrigerated. Warm on a dry tawa for 30 seconds a side before serving; never microwave, it turns rubbery.

recipes.name: Sabudana Khichdi
recipes.subtitle: tapioca pearls turned glassy in ghee with crushed peanuts and green chilli, the fasting-day standby

ingredients.note: the coating that keeps the pearls separate

ingredients.qty: 1 large, boiled and cut into 1cm dice

ingredients.note: leave out if you keep a strict fast

prepNotes: Rinse the sabudana three or four times until the water runs clear, then soak in water that sits just level with the pearls for 5 hours or overnight. Drowning them is what makes khichdi sticky.
Roast the peanuts and grind them coarse ahead of time — you want grit, not powder.
Boil and dice the potato before you start; it should be cool and firm.

steps.text: Check the soaked pearls: one should crush to a smooth paste between thumb and finger with no hard white centre. Drain in a colander for 10 minutes.
steps.tip: If the centres are still hard, sprinkle 2 tbsp water over, cover and wait another hour. Cooking will not rescue them.

steps.text: Toss the drained sabudana with the ground peanut, sugar and salt until every pearl is coated and the mix looks dry and loose.
Heat the ghee, add the cumin and let it darken for 20 seconds, then add the green chilli and curry leaves.
Add the diced potato and fry 2 minutes until the edges catch a little gold.
Tip in the sabudana, stir once to combine, then cook over medium heat for 5 to 7 minutes, turning it over gently every minute.
steps.tip: Stop the moment the pearls turn translucent. Beyond that they go chewy and clump into a single mass.

steps.text: Cover, take the pan off the heat and let it stand 2 minutes.
Squeeze over the lemon, fold through the coriander and serve hot, with a spoonful of plain yogurt alongside if you are not fasting.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight away. Refrigerated it hardens; reheat covered over low heat with a teaspoon of water and a little ghee for 3 minutes.

recipes.name: Sol Kadhi
recipes.subtitle: pink kokum and coconut milk drink, sour and cooling, drunk at the end of a coastal meal

ingredients.note: amsul; this is what makes it pink and sour

prepNotes: Soak the kokum petals in 250ml warm water for 20 minutes, then squeeze them out with your fingers and keep the pink liquid.
Use thick coconut milk, either the first press of freshly grated coconut or full-fat tinned.
Sol kadhi is served cold, so leave half an hour to chill it.

steps.text: Soak the kokum in the warm water 20 minutes, squeezing the petals every few minutes, until the water is a deep pink.
steps.tip: Do not boil the kokum. Heat dulls both the colour and the sourness.

steps.text: Squeeze the petals dry and discard them, keeping the pink extract.
Crush the garlic, green chilli and cumin to a rough paste with a pinch of salt.
Whisk the coconut milk with the remaining 300ml water until completely smooth and lump-free.
Stir the kokum extract into the coconut milk a little at a time, tasting as you go, until it is as sour as you want and a pale rose colour.
steps.tip: Add the acid to the coconut milk slowly and never the other way round, or it can split.

steps.text: Stir in the crushed garlic paste, salt and sugar, and let it stand 10 minutes for the garlic to bloom.
Chill 30 minutes, stir, scatter with coriander and serve in glasses, or poured over plain rice at the end of the meal.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated in a covered jar; the garlic gets stronger each day. Stir well before serving as it separates. Do not heat it.

recipes.name: Thalipeeth
recipes.subtitle: a savoury multigrain flatbread patted out by hand, spiced through and eaten with white butter

ingredients.note: the bhajani mix traditionally includes wheat
for the tawa

ingredients.qty: 2 tbsp, white butter if you can get it
ingredients.note: the traditional accompaniment
to serve

prepNotes: Mix the flours together first, on their own, so the proportions are even before anything wet goes in.
Have squares of parchment or banana leaf cut and ready — thalipeeth is patted out on the sheet, not rolled.
The dough wants 10 minutes of rest before you shape it, so the coarse flours drink the water.

steps.text: Combine the jowar, bajra, besan, rice flour and atta in a wide bowl with the salt.
Add the onion, coriander, green chilli, ginger, garlic, cumin, coriander powder, turmeric, chilli powder, ajwain and sesame and rub everything through the flour.
Pour in the warm water a little at a time and bring it together into a soft dough, softer than chapati dough and only just short of sticky.
steps.tip: A stiff dough cracks at the edges the moment you pat it out. Err wet.

steps.text: Cover and rest the dough 10 minutes, then divide into 6 balls.
Oil a square of parchment lightly, put a ball on it and pat it out with wet fingertips into a disc about 15cm across and 5mm thick.
steps.tip: Keep dipping your fingers in water. Dry fingers drag and tear the dough.

steps.text: Poke a hole through the middle with your finger and two or three smaller ones around it.
Invert the disc onto a hot tawa, peel away the parchment, and drizzle a teaspoon of oil into the centre hole and around the rim.
steps.tip: The hole is not decorative — it lets oil and heat reach the middle so it cooks through.

steps.text: Cover and cook 3 minutes over medium heat, then flip and cook a further 3 minutes uncovered until both sides carry dark brown spots.
Serve hot off the tawa with a lump of white butter melting on top and thick yogurt on the side.

recipes.storage: Thalipeeth is best straight off the tawa. Cooked ones keep 1 day wrapped in a cloth at room temperature and reheat on a dry tawa for a minute a side; the raw dough keeps 2 days refrigerated.

recipes.name: Ukadiche Modak
recipes.subtitle: Steamed rice-flour dumplings filled with coconut and jaggery, made for Ganpati

ingredients.note: use oil to keep it vegan

prepNotes: The dough must be kneaded hot. Let it cool and it cracks, and no amount of water will save it — keep a bowl of water beside you and work fast.
Fresh coconut only. Desiccated makes a dry, grainy filling.

steps.text: For the filling, cook the coconut and jaggery together over medium heat until the jaggery melts and the mixture comes together but is still moist, 8-10 minutes. Add cardamom, nutmeg and poppy seeds. Cool.
steps.tip: Stop while it is still moist; it hardens as it cools.

steps.text: Boil the water with a pinch of salt and a teaspoon of ghee. Take it off the heat, tip in the rice flour all at once and stir hard until no dry flour remains. Cover 5 minutes.
Turn out and knead while hot, greasing your palm with ghee, until completely smooth.
steps.tip: Hot dough. This is the step that decides whether modaks crack.

steps.text: Take a lime-sized ball, flatten into a cup with your fingers, pleat the edge into 9-11 folds, fill, then gather the pleats to a point and seal.
Steam 10-12 minutes until the shells turn glossy and translucent.
Serve warm with a spoon of ghee over the top.

recipes.storage: Best within a few hours. Keeps a day refrigerated but the shell hardens; steam 3-4 minutes to soften before serving. Do not freeze.

recipes.name: Vada Pav
recipes.subtitle: Mumbai's potato fritter in a bun, with garlic chutney and fried chillies

ingredients.note: for the batter
omit from the chutney for a nut-free version
for the chutney
for the chutney

prepNotes: Mash the potato coarsely, leaving some lumps. A smooth mash makes a pasty vada.
The batter should coat the back of a spoon thickly. Too thin and it slides off in the oil; too thick and it fries into a shell.
The dry garlic chutney is not optional in Mumbai. It is what makes the sandwich taste like vada pav rather than a potato bun.

steps.text: For the dry chutney, dry roast the peanuts, coconut and 6 garlic cloves separately until fragrant, then grind coarsely with the chilli powder and salt. Set aside.
Crush the remaining garlic, the green chillies and ginger to a coarse paste.

Heat 2 tbsp oil, splutter the mustard seeds, add the asafoetida and curry leaves, then the garlic-chilli paste. Fry 1 minute, add the turmeric, then fold through the mashed potato, coriander, lemon and salt. Cool and shape into 8 balls.
Whisk the besan with a pinch of turmeric, salt and enough water to make a thick, smooth coating batter. Rest it 10 minutes.
Heat the frying oil to 180C. Dip each ball in batter, let the excess drip off and lower it in. Fry 4-5 minutes until pale gold and crisp, turning once. Drain on a rack, not paper.
steps.tip: Fry a few whole green chillies alongside; slit them first so they do not burst.

steps.text: Split the pav without cutting all the way through, spread the dry chutney generously inside, press in a hot vada and serve at once with the fried chillies.

recipes.storage: Eat immediately; this does not keep well assembled. The potato mixture can be made a day ahead and refrigerated, and fried vadas reheat acceptably in a hot oven for 6-8 minutes.

recipes.name: Varan Bhaat
recipes.subtitle: plain toor dal with ghee and a touch of jaggery over hot rice, the first course of every festive meal

ingredients.note: use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
half in the dal, half poured over the rice

ingredients.qty: 700ml for the dal, 600ml for the rice

prepNotes: Rinse the dal in three changes of water until it runs clear, then soak 20 minutes so it cooks evenly.
Rinse and soak the rice 15 minutes as well; varan bhaat is eaten with soft, loose grains.
Varan carries no onion, garlic or chilli by design. Do not be tempted to improve it.

steps.text: Rinse and soak the toor dal 20 minutes, then drain.
Pressure cook the dal with 500ml water and the turmeric for 4 whistles, or simmer covered 40 minutes, until it collapses at a touch.
Cook the rice in the remaining water until soft, about 15 minutes, and keep it covered and hot.
Open the cooker and whisk the dal smooth with a ladle, adding the remaining 200ml water until it pours easily.
steps.tip: Varan should be thin enough to soak into rice, not thick enough to stand a spoon in.

steps.text: Bring it back to a simmer with the salt, jaggery and hing and cook 5 minutes.
steps.tip: The jaggery is not there to sweeten it, only to round the edge. Two teaspoons is plenty.

steps.text: Heat the ghee, crackle the cumin seeds if using, and pour it into the dal.
Squeeze in the lemon off the heat and taste for salt.
Serve a ladle of varan over a mound of hot rice with a spoon of raw ghee on top, and eat it first, before anything else on the plate.

recipes.storage: The varan keeps 3 days refrigerated and thickens; loosen with hot water and re-season. Cooked rice keeps 2 days — steam it back to life rather than microwaving it dry.

recipes.name: Zunka
recipes.subtitle: dry crumbled gram flour cooked with onion and garlic, sharp with green chilli

ingredients.note: use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Dry-roast the besan first and let it cool — this is what separates zunka from a bowl of raw-tasting paste.
Boil the water before you start. Cold water into hot besan sets lumps instantly.
Chop the onion fine; big pieces stay wet and the zunka will not crumble.

steps.text: Dry-roast the besan in the pan over low heat for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring, until it turns a shade darker and smells nutty. Tip it out and let it cool.
steps.tip: Besan scorches at the bottom while the top still looks pale. Keep it moving.

steps.text: Heat the oil, add the mustard seeds and wait for them to pop, then the cumin, curry leaves and hing.
Add the onion and cook 5 minutes over medium heat until soft and translucent — soft, not browned.
Stir in the garlic and green chilli and fry 1 minute.
Add the turmeric, chilli powder and salt, then pour in the hot water and bring it to a boil.
Lower the heat and sprinkle the roasted besan over the surface in a thin stream with one hand while stirring hard with the other.
steps.tip: Sprinkle, never dump. A single spoonful tipped in at once becomes a lump you cannot break up.

steps.text: Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 5 minutes without stirring, then take the lid off and break the mass up with a fork into a coarse crumble.
Drizzle over a spoonful of raw oil, fold through the coriander and serve with jowar bhakri and raw onion.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat covered over low heat with a sprinkle of water for 3 minutes; do not microwave it dry or it turns to sand.

recipes.name: Aloo Pitika
recipes.subtitle: mashed potato sharpened with raw mustard oil and onion, the plate-partner to every assamese meal

ingredients.note: unheated is the whole point — the pungency is the seasoning

prepNotes: Boil the potatoes whole and in their skins. Peeled and cubed, they take on water and the pitika goes wet and gluey.
Chop the onion as fine as you can and, if raw onion bothers you, soak it in cold water 5 minutes and squeeze it dry before it goes in.
Have the mustard oil at room temperature. It never sees heat in this dish.

steps.text: Boil the whole potatoes in well-salted water 20 minutes, until a knife slides to the centre with no push.
steps.tip: Start them in cold water so they cook evenly rather than splitting at the edges.

steps.text: Drain and peel them while still hot — the skins slip off between your fingers.
Mash with your hand or a fork while warm, leaving a little texture. Do not use a blender.
steps.tip: A blender works the starch and turns the mash to glue within seconds.

steps.text: Pour the raw mustard oil straight over the warm mash and work it in until the mash looks glossy and smells sharp.
Fold in the onion, green chilli, coriander and salt.
Add the lemon juice, taste, and correct the salt — it needs more than you think against the plain rice it is eaten with.
Shape into a low mound on the plate and let it stand 5 minutes so the onion softens into the potato.

recipes.storage: Best the day it is made, but keeps 2 days refrigerated. Bring it back to room temperature before serving and refresh it with a teaspoon of raw mustard oil — do not reheat, it goes pasty.

recipes.name: Axone Pork
recipes.subtitle: naga pork belly stewed to spoon-softness with fermented funk and raw chilli heat

ingredients.qty: 800g belly, skin on, cut into 3cm cubes

ingredients.note: axone, the fermented soybean cake this dish is named for, has no equivalent in the catalogue; dried fish gives the same fermented savoury backbone, though the aroma is different — if you can find axone, use 2 tbsp instead
for raja mircha, the Naga king chilli; two fresh bird's-eye chillies alongside gets you closer
not traditional everywhere, but common in Kohima kitchens
fresh or brined; rinse brined shoot twice

prepNotes: Use belly with a decent fat cap. Lean pork gives a thin, joyless version of this dish — the rendered fat is the cooking medium and there is no added oil.
Rinse the dried fish twice in warm water, pat it dry, and dry-roast it 3 minutes before it goes in.
Naga cooking uses no oil and almost no dry spice here. The flavour comes entirely from pork fat, ferment, ginger and chilli, so all four have to be good.

steps.text: Put the pork cubes in a heavy dry pot over medium heat with 2 tbsp of the water and cook 10 minutes, turning, until the fat has rendered and the cubes are browning in their own fat.
steps.tip: No oil goes into this pot at any stage. If it sticks in the first two minutes, add a spoon of water, not fat.

steps.text: Add the onion, garlic and half the ginger and fry 5 minutes in the rendered fat, until the onion has gone soft and translucent.
Stir in the torn dried chillies and the roasted dried fish and fry 2 minutes, until the whole pot smells sharp and savoury.
steps.tip: This is the moment the kitchen turns pungent. That smell mellowing into the pork over the next hour is the point of the dish.

steps.text: Add the tomato, if using, and cook 3 minutes until it breaks down.
Pour in the rest of the water, add salt, cover and simmer very gently 45 minutes. Check at 30 minutes and add a splash if it looks dry.
Add the bamboo shoot and the green chillies and simmer uncovered 10 minutes more.
The pork is ready when a piece of skin gives completely under a spoon and the gravy has reduced to a thick, glossy few centimetres in the base.
steps.tip: If it is still chewy, it needs time, not heat — go another 15 minutes covered on low.

steps.text: Stir in the remaining ginger julienne and the spring onion, rest 5 minutes off the heat, and serve with plain sticky rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and improves overnight as the ferment settles into the fat. Lift off the set fat cap, reheat gently on the stovetop, and add fresh ginger and spring onion at the end.

recipes.name: Bai
recipes.subtitle: the mizo pot of greens and pumpkin, barely seasoned and softened with an alkaline pinch

ingredients.note: any sturdy local green does — this is what most kitchens use
fermented bamboo shoot is the classic addition; rinse brined shoot well or it dominates
the corm; peel it under running water and cook it right through
stands in for chingal, the alkaline water Mizo cooks filter through wood ash; the catalogue has no chingal and this is the closest thing

prepNotes: Bai has no onion, no garlic and no oil. That is not an omission — the point is the taste of the vegetables themselves, so buy them fresh and cut them the same day.
A quarter teaspoon of baking soda is plenty. Too much and the greens go slimy and the pot smells faintly of soap.
Peel colocasia under running water and rinse your hands after; the raw corm can itch.

steps.text: Bring the water to a boil in a wide pot with the salt, slit chillies and ginger.
Add the colocasia, if using, and boil 10 minutes — it takes longer than everything else and must be cooked right through.
steps.tip: Undercooked colocasia is unpleasantly scratchy in the throat. Give it the full time.

steps.text: Add the pumpkin and boil 6 minutes, until the edges have just started to soften.
Add the beans and bamboo shoot and cook 4 minutes.
Pile in the mustard greens, push them under the liquid and cook 4 minutes, until they have collapsed and turned dark.
Stir in the baking soda and simmer 3 minutes more. The greens will soften noticeably and the broth thickens a little.
steps.tip: It goes in at the end. Added at the start it strips the colour out of the greens.

steps.text: Crush a few pieces of pumpkin against the side of the pot to thicken the liquid, taste for salt, and serve hot with rice and a chilli chutney.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated, though the alkali keeps working and the greens will be softer on day two. Reheat gently on the stovetop with a splash of water; do not boil hard.

recipes.name: Chamthong
recipes.subtitle: the manipuri everyday vegetable stew, clear and light and lifted by fermented fish

ingredients.note: any soft local green does; this is what goes in at home
stands in for ngari, Manipuri fermented fish — dry-roast it first; the catalogue carries no ngari
chamthong is a near-oilless broth; this is all it gets

prepNotes: Dry-roast the dried fish for 3 minutes over low heat before it goes in. Straight from the packet it makes the broth muddy.
Cut the vegetables to roughly the same size and add them in order of hardness — this stew is boiled, not layered with fat, so timing is the only thing keeping it from turning to soup.
Chamthong is deliberately plain. Resist adding garlic or masala: it is meant to sit next to eromba and a chilli chutney, not compete with them.

steps.text: Dry-roast the dried fish 3 minutes over low heat until brittle and toasty, then break it into rough pieces.
Bring the water to a boil in a wide pot with the onion, ginger, green chillies, roasted fish and salt. Boil 5 minutes.
Add the potato and pumpkin and boil 8 minutes, uncovered, until the potato is nearly done.
steps.tip: Uncovered — a lid makes the greens go grey later and dulls the whole pot.

steps.text: Add the beans and cook 4 minutes.
Add the cabbage and cook 3 minutes, until it has just wilted but still has a bite.
Stir in the amaranth greens and the tablespoon of oil and cook 2 minutes more.
steps.tip: The oil goes in at the end; it sits on top as a few bright beads rather than dissolving into the broth.

steps.text: Taste for salt, scatter over the spring onion and serve hot in bowls alongside rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat only to a bare simmer — a hard boil turns the pumpkin to purée and the greens to sludge. Add the spring onion fresh each time.

recipes.name: Doh Khleh
recipes.subtitle: khasi pork salad — boiled meat tossed hot with onion, chilli and a lot of lemon

ingredients.qty: 500g belly or shoulder, in one piece

ingredients.note: doh khleh should be properly sharp
black sesame is what is used in Meghalaya; the catalogue's sesame is the same seed, so roast it a shade darker
for the boiling water

prepNotes: Boil the pork in one piece and dice it after — diced first, it dries out and loses its bounce.
Slice the onion paper-thin and salt it while the pork boils. Twenty minutes of sitting takes the harshness out.
Dress the salad while the pork is still warm. Cold meat will not take up the lemon.

steps.text: Bring the water to a boil with the bay leaf and a generous tablespoon of salt, lower in the pork and simmer 35 minutes.
Test it with a skewer — it should go in easily but the meat should still hold together, not shred.
steps.tip: Boil it past this point and the salad turns to threads.

steps.text: Meanwhile toss the sliced onion with a big pinch of salt and leave it in a bowl for 20 minutes.
Roast the sesame in a dry pan 2 minutes, until it pops and smells toasted, then grind it coarsely.
Lift the pork out, rest it 5 minutes, then cut it into 1.5cm dice, fat and all.
While it is still warm, toss the pork with the onion and any liquid in its bowl, the ginger, green chilli and crushed black pepper.
Add the lemon juice and check the salt — the boiling water has seasoned the meat already, so taste before adding more.
steps.tip: Add the lemon to warm meat, not hot: straight off the boil it just evaporates.

steps.text: Fold in the ground sesame and coriander and serve at room temperature, on its own or with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated but the onion softens and the lemon fades. Bring it to room temperature and refresh with a squeeze of lemon and fresh coriander; do not reheat.

recipes.name: Eromba
recipes.subtitle: manipuri mash of boiled vegetables, fierce chilli and fermented fish, eaten with rice

ingredients.note: stands in for ngari, the Manipuri fermented fish; the catalogue has no ngari, and dried fish rinsed and dry-roasted gives the closest savoury weight
for umorok, the local king chilli; use three if you want to live
the nearest thing to maroi napakpi, the Manipuri hill chive

prepNotes: Rinse the dried fish twice in warm water and pat it dry before roasting, or the eromba comes out salty and rank rather than savoury.
Eromba is a mash, not a curry — it should hold its shape on the spoon. Boil the vegetables in as little water as will cover them.
Everything gets pounded together at the end, so cut the vegetables large; they only need to be soft.

steps.text: Dry-roast the dried fish in a small pan over low heat for 3 minutes, turning, until it smells toasty and goes brittle. Crumble it and set aside.
steps.tip: Low heat and keep it moving — scorched dried fish tastes of nothing but burnt.

steps.text: Roast the dried red chillies in the same pan 40 seconds a side, until they darken and puff slightly. Pound them to a coarse paste with a pinch of salt.
steps.tip: Open a window. Roasting this many chillies will clear the room.

steps.text: Boil the potato in the water for 8 minutes.
Add the eggplant and beans and boil 8 minutes more, until everything is completely tender and the potato is starting to fall apart.
Drain, keeping about 100ml of the cooking water.
Mash the vegetables roughly in the pot with the back of a ladle, leaving some lumps.
Work in the crumbled fish, the chilli paste and salt, adding the reserved water a spoon at a time until it is thick and scoopable.
Fold in the spring onion and coriander off the heat and serve at room temperature with hot rice.
steps.tip: The greens go in raw at the end — cooked, they lose the sharp note the mash is built around.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Serve at room temperature rather than reheated; if it has stiffened, loosen it with a tablespoon of warm water and fresh chopped spring onion.

recipes.name: Hanhor Mangkho
recipes.subtitle: assamese duck stewed slowly with ash gourd, peppery and lean rather than creamy

ingredients.qty: 1kg, on the bone, cut into curry pieces

ingredients.note: the traditional partner; it drinks up the fat
pepper carries this curry, not chilli powder — crush it fresh

prepNotes: Duck carries a lot of fat under the skin. Dry-fry the pieces first with no oil for a few minutes and pour off what renders, or the curry sits under a slick.
Grind the ginger and garlic fresh into a coarse paste — a duck this strongly flavoured flattens shop-bought paste.
Ash gourd goes in only for the last stretch. Added early it dissolves completely.

steps.text: Put the duck pieces in a dry heavy pot over medium heat and cook 6 minutes, turning, until fat pools in the base. Pour that fat off and set the duck aside.
steps.tip: This one step is the difference between a clean curry and a greasy one.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in the same pot until it smokes, cool it a minute, then fry the bay leaf, cinnamon, cloves and black cardamom for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the sliced onion and cook 12 minutes over medium heat, until deep gold and shrunk to a third of its volume.
steps.tip: Do not rush this — pale onion leaves the curry thin and sweetish.

steps.text: Stir in the ginger and garlic paste and fry 3 minutes, until the raw smell goes and the oil starts to separate at the edges.
Add the turmeric and crushed black pepper, stir for 20 seconds, then return the duck and toss to coat every piece.
Fry the duck in the masala 8 minutes, scraping the base as it catches, until the pieces are browned all over.
Pour in the hot water, add salt, cover and simmer very gently 45 minutes, until a skewer goes into the thigh with no resistance.
Add the ash gourd and green chillies and simmer uncovered 15 minutes more, until the gourd is translucent and the gravy has reduced to a coating consistency.
steps.tip: Translucent, not collapsed — check at 10 minutes, it can go from firm to mush quickly.

steps.text: Rest 10 minutes off the heat before serving with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and is better on the second day. Skim the set fat from the top before reheating, then warm gently on the stovetop with a few spoons of water.

recipes.name: Jadoh
recipes.subtitle: khasi rice cooked through with pork, ginger and black pepper, meghalaya's one-pot meal

ingredients.qty: 300g short-grain, washed until the water runs clear
ingredients.note: Khasi red rice is what is used at home; any short-grain rice works

ingredients.qty: 400g belly or shoulder with its fat, cut into 1cm dice

ingredients.note: jadoh is a gingery dish; do not cut this back
only to start the pork off; it renders plenty of its own

prepNotes: Wash the rice until the water runs clear and soak it 20 minutes, then drain it well. Wet rice going into hot fat clumps.

Traditional jadoh is cooked with pig's blood, which is what gives it the dark colour you see in Shillong stalls. This version leaves it out; the turmeric version is common at home and in Khasi restaurants.
Get the pork diced small — 1cm — so it cooks in the same time as the rice.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a heavy pot and fry the diced pork over medium-high heat for 8 minutes, until it has rendered its fat and the edges are browned and crisp.
steps.tip: Crowd the pot and it steams instead of browning. Use a wide pan and give it room.

steps.text: Add the bay leaves and sliced onion and cook 8 minutes in the pork fat, until the onion is gold and sticky.
Stir in the ginger and garlic and fry 2 minutes, until the raw edge has gone.
Add the turmeric and crushed black pepper and stir for 30 seconds.
Tip in the drained rice and toss gently for 3 minutes, until every grain is coated and glossy and the rice smells toasted.
steps.tip: Fold rather than stir — a spoon dragged through soaked rice snaps the grains.

steps.text: Pour in the hot water, add the green chillies and salt, and bring to a fast boil.
As soon as the water level drops to the surface of the rice, cover tightly, drop the heat to its lowest and cook 12 minutes undisturbed.
steps.tip: No peeking. Lifting the lid lets out the steam that is doing the cooking.

steps.text: Take it off the heat and rest, still covered, 10 minutes. Fluff with a fork, scatter over the spring onion and serve.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat covered with a tablespoon of water sprinkled over the top, on low heat or in a steamer, so the grains soften rather than dry out.

recipes.name: Masor Tenga
recipes.subtitle: assam's daily sour fish curry, thin and lemon-bright rather than rich

ingredients.qty: 600g rohu or any firm river fish, cut into 2cm steaks

ingredients.note: the defining fat here — no other oil gives the same pungency
the everyday souring agent; dried thekera or elephant apple is used when in season
usual in home kitchens, and it thickens the broth a little
goes in off the heat

prepNotes: Rub the fish with half the turmeric and a good pinch of salt and leave it 15 minutes. This firms the surface so the steaks do not shred in the pan.
Heat mustard oil until it smokes and goes pale, then pull it off the heat for a minute before frying. Raw mustard oil tastes harsh and stays that way.
Tenga means sour. Tomato is what most Assamese kitchens use on a weekday; if you have dried thekera, use two pieces and cut back to one tomato.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a wide pan until it smokes, take it off the heat for a minute, then fry the fish steaks 2 minutes a side until the edges are golden. Lift them out onto a plate.
steps.tip: Do not move them for the first 2 minutes — the skin sticks and tears if you fuss.

steps.text: In the same oil, crackle the fenugreek seeds for about 10 seconds, until they darken a shade and smell nutty.
steps.tip: Fenugreek turns bitter fast. Count to ten and move straight on.

steps.text: Slide in the potato wedges and fry 4 minutes, until the cut edges look translucent.
Add the tomato, the rest of the turmeric, the slit chillies and salt. Cook 5 minutes, pressing the tomato with the back of the spoon, until it slumps and gives up its water.
Pour in the water, bring to a boil and simmer 10 minutes uncovered, until the potato gives easily to a knife.
Slide the fish back in, spoon broth over each piece and simmer 4 minutes more. Shake the pan rather than stirring.
steps.tip: Stirring at this point breaks the fish into the broth.

steps.text: Take the pan off the heat, stir in the lemon juice and coriander, and let it sit 5 minutes before serving over plain rice.
steps.tip: Lemon goes in off the heat — boiled, it flattens and turns faintly bitter.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated and the sourness deepens overnight. Reheat gently in a wide pan without stirring, loosening with a splash of water and a fresh squeeze of lemon.

recipes.name: Momos
recipes.subtitle: Steamed dumplings with a juicy filling, eaten with a fiery tomato-chilli chutney

ingredients.note: or finely chopped cabbage for a vegetarian version
for the chutney
for the chutney

prepNotes: Everything in the filling must be chopped very fine and kept raw — it cooks in the steamer, and any large piece will tear the wrapper.
Do not salt the filling until just before you fill: salt draws water out of the cabbage and makes the dough soggy.

steps.text: Knead the flour with water and a pinch of salt into a firm, smooth dough. Rest 30 minutes covered.
Mix the filling ingredients with the oil and pepper. Salt it only when you are ready to fill.
Roll the dough very thin and cut 8cm rounds, keeping the edges thinner than the centre.
steps.tip: Thin edges, thicker middle — otherwise the pleated top is doughy.

steps.text: Place a spoon of filling in each, then pleat and seal into a half-moon or a gathered purse.
Steam in a greased steamer for 10-12 minutes. The wrappers turn translucent and stop looking floury.
steps.tip: Do not crowd them; they swell and stick together.

steps.text: For the chutney, boil the tomatoes and dried chillies, then blend with garlic and salt. Serve alongside.

recipes.storage: Best straight from the steamer. Uncooked momos freeze well on a tray for a month — steam from frozen, adding 4 minutes. Cooked ones go rubbery.

recipes.name: Muya Awandru
recipes.subtitle: tripura's oil-free bamboo shoot pot, thickened with rice flour and pungent with dried fish

ingredients.qty: 300g, fresh or brined, rinsed twice and sliced thin

ingredients.note: stands in for berma, the dry fermented fish at the heart of Tripuri mui borok cooking; the catalogue carries no berma
the thickener — slake it in cold water before it goes anywhere near the pot
Tripuri food is genuinely hot; four is a compromise

ingredients.qty: 800ml, plus 4 tbsp cold for the slurry

prepNotes: Brined bamboo shoot needs rinsing twice and a 5-minute boil in fresh water before you start, or the whole pot tastes only of brine.
Slake the rice flour in 4 tbsp of cold water and stir it smooth before it goes in. Tipped in dry it seizes into lumps that never dissolve.
This is cooked without a drop of oil, which is the defining habit of mui borok. Do not be tempted to start with a tempering.

steps.text: Rinse the bamboo shoot twice, cover with fresh water, boil 5 minutes and drain.
steps.tip: Skip this and the sourness of the brine flattens everything else in the pot.

steps.text: Dry-roast the dried fish in a small pan over low heat 3 minutes, until brittle and toasty, then break it into pieces.
Bring the 800ml of water to a boil with the crushed ginger, garlic, green chillies, roasted fish and salt. Boil 5 minutes so the broth takes on the flavours.
Add the drained bamboo shoot and the potato and simmer 12 minutes, uncovered.
Add the beans and cook 5 minutes, until the potato is soft enough to break with a spoon.
Stir the rice flour into 4 tbsp cold water until completely smooth, with no dry specks.
steps.tip: Cold water only. Warm water starts cooking the flour in the cup.

steps.text: Pour the slurry into the simmering pot in a thin stream, stirring the whole time, and cook 4 minutes until the liquid turns glossy and coats the back of a spoon.
Taste for salt and heat, stir in the coriander and serve hot with plain rice.
steps.tip: It thickens further as it cools — take it off the heat looser than you want it.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated but sets firm as the rice flour cools. Reheat on low with 3-4 tbsp of water, stirring until it loosens back to a coating consistency.

recipes.name: Naga Smoked Pork with Bamboo Shoot
recipes.subtitle: Smoked pork simmered with fermented bamboo shoot and raja mircha

image.alt: Naga smoked pork with bamboo shoot

ingredients.note: raja mircha traditionally — use far less

prepNotes: Naga cooking uses very little oil and few spices; the flavour is carried by smoke, fermentation and heat. Adding garam masala here would be a mistake.
Fermented bamboo shoot is pungent. Rinse it, and add it in stages, tasting as you go.

steps.text: Rinse the fermented bamboo shoot in two changes of water and drain.
Put the smoked pork in a pot with the ginger, garlic, chillies and just enough water to cover. Bring to a boil.
steps.tip: No oil. The pork renders plenty of its own.

steps.text: Simmer covered 45-60 minutes until the pork is tender and the water has reduced by half.
Add the bamboo shoot and the onion and tomato if using, and cook a further 15 minutes.
steps.tip: Taste before adding all the bamboo — its sourness varies enormously between batches.

steps.text: Season with salt only at the end; smoked pork is already salty.
Serve with plain rice and a raw chilli on the side.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and improves. Freezes 2 months.

recipes.name: Omita Khar
recipes.subtitle: the alkaline assamese opener — raw papaya simmered soft, plain and cleansing

ingredients.qty: 500g, peeled, deseeded and cut into 3cm cubes

ingredients.note: stands in for khar, the alkaline water filtered through sun-dried banana-peel ash; the catalogue has no khar and this is the standard urban substitute
fried till golden, the upper-Assam habit

prepNotes: A quarter teaspoon of baking soda is the ceiling for this quantity. More and the dish turns soapy and slippery on the tongue — there is no fixing it once it is in.
Soak the whole urad 30 minutes and drain it thoroughly on a cloth, or it will spit in the hot oil.
Khar is eaten first, at the very start of an Assamese meal, with plain rice and nothing sour alongside it.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a heavy pan until it smokes, then let it cool for a minute.
Fry the drained urad 2 minutes until deep gold and lift it out with a slotted spoon. Keep it for the end.
steps.tip: It should crackle, not brown in seconds — if it darkens instantly the oil is still too hot.

steps.text: Drop in the slit chillies and let them blister 30 seconds.
Add the papaya, turmeric and salt and toss 3 minutes, until the cut edges look glassy.
Pour in the water, cover and simmer 12 minutes, until a fork goes through a cube with no resistance.
Stir in the baking soda and simmer uncovered 5 minutes. It will foam up and settle, and the liquid turns faintly silky.
steps.tip: Add it at the end, never at the start — early alkali collapses the papaya to mush.

steps.text: Crush four or five cubes against the side of the pan to thicken the broth, then scatter over the fried urad and coriander and serve at once.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated, and the alkali keeps softening the papaya, so it will be looser on day two. Reheat gently with a splash of water; add the fried urad fresh if you want the crunch back.

recipes.name: Singju
recipes.subtitle: manipur's raw-vegetable salad bound with roasted gram flour and loud with chilli

ingredients.qty: 250g, shredded as finely as you can manage

ingredients.note: dry-roasted; this is the binder that makes singju singju
stands in for thoiding, the perilla seed used in Manipur, which the catalogue does not carry — roast and grind it the same way
for ngari, the fermented fish; roast and crumble it

prepNotes: Shred the cabbage on the day and keep it dry. Washed and not spun out, the water thins the gram flour and the salad slumps.
Roast the besan, sesame, chilli and dried fish ahead — all four can be done in the same pan, in that order, in under ten minutes.
Dress it at the last minute. Singju is assembled to be eaten within about twenty minutes.

steps.text: Dry-roast the besan over low heat for 4 minutes, stirring constantly, until it turns a shade darker and smells nutty. Tip it straight out of the pan.
steps.tip: It goes from nutty to burnt in about fifteen seconds at the end. Do not walk away.

steps.text: Roast the sesame in the same pan 2 minutes until the seeds start popping, then grind them coarsely.
Roast the dried red chillies 40 seconds a side until they darken, and pound them coarse.
Roast the dried fish 3 minutes over low heat until brittle, then crumble it fine.
Toss the cabbage, radish and spring onion in a wide bowl with the salt and leave 5 minutes.
Squeeze the vegetables gently with your hands and pour off any water that has come out.
steps.tip: This is the step people skip, and it is why home singju often goes soggy.

steps.text: Scatter over the roasted besan, ground sesame, crumbled fish and pounded chilli, and mix with your fingers until every shred is coated and the flour has stopped looking powdery.
Add the lemon juice and coriander, toss once more and serve immediately as a side or an evening snack.

recipes.storage: Eat within the hour — the gram flour draws water and the salad wilts. The roasted besan, sesame, chilli and fish keep a week in an airtight jar, so make that mix ahead and shred the cabbage fresh.

recipes.name: Thukpa
recipes.subtitle: sikkim's hand-torn noodle soup, chicken broth thick with vegetables and pepper

ingredients.note: for hand-pulled noodles; 300g of ready wheat noodles works if you would rather not

ingredients.qty: 400g boneless thigh, cut into thin strips
1.2 litres for the broth, plus about 120ml for the dough

prepNotes: Make the dough first and let it rest 30 minutes before you touch it again. Unrested, it springs back and you will fight it the whole time.
Have every vegetable cut before the broth goes on. Once the noodles are in, this dish moves in under five minutes.
Cook the noodles in the soup, not separately. The starch they release is what gives thukpa its body.

steps.text: Mix the maida with 1/2 tsp salt and enough water — about 120ml — to make a firm, slightly stiff dough. Knead 8 minutes until smooth, then cover and rest 30 minutes.
steps.tip: Firmer than a chapati dough. A soft dough tears into shapeless scraps in the broth.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot and fry the onion, garlic and ginger 5 minutes over medium heat, until the onion is soft and the garlic smells sweet.
Add the chicken strips and fry 5 minutes, until they have lost their pink and picked up a little colour at the edges.
Stir in the turmeric, chilli powder and crushed black pepper for 20 seconds, then add the tomato and cook 5 minutes until it collapses.
Pour in the 1.2 litres of water, add salt, and simmer 15 minutes with the lid ajar.
While it simmers, roll the rested dough out to about 2mm and cut or tear it into ribbons roughly 2cm wide and 10cm long. Dust them with flour and keep them separate.
steps.tip: Torn edges hold the broth better than knife-cut ones, which is why thenthuk is torn by hand.

steps.text: Add the carrot to the simmering broth and cook 3 minutes.
Drop the noodles in a few at a time, stirring so they do not clump, and boil 4 minutes until they float and turn from chalky to translucent.
steps.tip: A few at a time, into moving liquid. Dumped in together they weld into a single mass.

steps.text: Add the cabbage and spinach and cook 2 minutes more, until the spinach has just wilted.
Taste for salt and pepper, ladle into deep bowls and finish with spring onion and coriander.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight away — the noodles keep swelling and drink the broth. If you want leftovers, cook and store the broth separately for up to 3 days and boil fresh noodles into a reheated portion.

recipes.name: Aloo Potala Rasa
recipes.subtitle: potato and pointed gourd in a thin, cumin-scented tomato gravy, made without onion or garlic

ingredients.note: potala, or parwal

prepNotes: Scrape the pointed gourd lightly with a knife rather than peeling it — the skin holds the flavour and stops the pieces going mushy.
Puree the tomatoes and grate the ginger before you start. With no onion or garlic in this dish, the tomato has to be fried properly and that needs your full attention.
Cut the potato into quarters, not smaller; they should stay in recognisable pieces in the thin gravy.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes, then lower the flame for 30 seconds.
Fry the halved pointed gourd on medium for 5 minutes, turning, until blistered and lightly browned. Lift out and set aside.
steps.tip: Frying them separately keeps them firm; boiled straight into the gravy they go limp.

steps.text: In the same oil add the bay leaf and cumin seeds and let them sizzle 15 seconds.
Add the grated ginger and slit green chillies and fry 1 minute.
Add the potato quarters and fry 4 minutes until the edges are golden.
Pour in the tomato puree with the turmeric, cumin powder, coriander powder, chilli powder and salt. Fry 6-8 minutes until the oil beads at the edges.
steps.tip: Do not shortcut this. Underfried tomato leaves the gravy tasting sour and raw.

steps.text: Add the water, bring to a boil, then cover and simmer 12 minutes until the potato is tender.
Return the fried pointed gourd and simmer uncovered 5 minutes. The gravy should stay thin — this is a rasa, not a thick curry.
Stir in the garam masala, scatter the coriander leaves and rest 5 minutes off the heat before serving with rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat on the stovetop with 3 tbsp water; the pointed gourd softens further overnight but the flavour deepens.

recipes.name: Besara
recipes.subtitle: mixed vegetables in a sharp ground-mustard gravy, pungent enough to make your eyes water

ingredients.qty: 2 tbsp, soaked in warm water 20 minutes
ingredients.note: the whole dish is named for this
ground into the mustard paste
2 for the paste, 1 slit for the pot

prepNotes: Soak the mustard seeds in warm water for at least 20 minutes before grinding. Unsoaked seeds grind unevenly and taste bitter rather than hot.
Grind the mustard with the garlic, 2 green chillies and a pinch of salt to a fine paste with 4 tbsp water. Salt in the grinder keeps the paste from turning bitter.
Cut the vegetables into even 2-3cm pieces so nothing collapses while the slower pieces cook.

steps.text: Grind the soaked mustard seeds, garlic, 2 green chillies and a pinch of salt to a smooth paste with 4 tbsp water. Set aside.
steps.tip: Grind in short bursts. Long continuous grinding heats the paste and makes it acrid.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes, then lower the flame for 30 seconds.
Add the panch phoron and broken dried red chillies. When the seeds pop and the chillies darken, about 20 seconds, add the slit green chilli.
Add the potato and raw banana and fry 3 minutes, stirring, until the surfaces turn matte.
Add the pumpkin, eggplant and drumstick with the turmeric and salt. Fry 2 minutes more.
Pour in the water, bring to a boil, cover and simmer 12 minutes until the potato is nearly tender.
Lower the flame to its weakest setting and stir in the mustard paste. Do not let it boil hard from here on.
steps.tip: Boiling ground mustard hard is the classic besara mistake — it turns the gravy bitter within a minute.

steps.text: Simmer uncovered on low for 6-8 minutes, until the raw smell of the mustard has gone and the gravy coats a spoon.
Taste for salt, stir in the coriander leaves and take off the heat. Rest 5 minutes before serving with rice.

recipes.storage: Best the day it is made — the mustard sharpens overnight. Keeps 2 days refrigerated; reheat on the lowest flame with a splash of water and never let it boil.

recipes.name: Chhena Poda
recipes.subtitle: Odisha's baked cheesecake: fresh chhena and sugar caramelised until the top is almost burnt

ingredients.note: separate from the sugar above

prepNotes: Poda means burnt. The dark, almost-scorched top is the dish, not a mistake — pull it out pale and it is just baked cheese.
Chhena for this should be soft and moist. Unlike rasgulla, do not hang it dry.

steps.text: Curdle the milk with lemon juice, strain through muslin and rinse briefly. Hang only 20 minutes — it should stay moist.
Knead the chhena smooth, then work in the sugar, rava, cardamom, nuts and raisins. Rest 15 minutes so the rava swells.
Caramelise the 2 tbsp sugar in a ghee-greased tin and let it set at the bottom.
steps.tip: Traditionally the batter sits on a lining of sal leaves, which is where the smoky note comes from.

steps.text: Pour in the batter and bake at 180C for 50-60 minutes, until the top is deep brown to nearly black and a skewer comes out clean.
steps.tip: Go further than instinct says. Brown is not enough.

steps.text: Cool completely in the tin — at least 2 hours — before turning out.
Serve at room temperature in wedges.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and firms as it sits. Bring back to room temperature before serving; cold chhena poda tastes flat.

recipes.name: Chhena Tarkari
recipes.subtitle: soft fresh cheese in a light gingered tomato gravy, no onion, no garlic, straight out of the temple kitchen

ingredients.note: or fresh chhena, drained and pressed only lightly so it stays soft
the only aromatic in the dish, so use it generously
added at the end
softens the gravy the way cream would

prepNotes: If you are using shop paneer, soak the cubes in hot salted water for 10 minutes before you start. It brings back the softness that chhena has naturally.
Puree the tomatoes smooth and keep them ready; with no onion in the pan, the tomato has to be fried properly to build the base.
Grate the ginger rather than chopping it so it melts into the gravy.

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a kadhai and add the bay leaf and cumin seeds. They should sizzle on contact and smell toasty in about 15 seconds.
Add the grated ginger and slit green chillies and fry 1 minute, until the raw ginger smell lifts.
Pour in the tomato puree with the turmeric, cumin powder and coriander powder. Stand back — it will spit.
Fry the puree on medium heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring, until it darkens to brick red and the ghee separates at the edges.
steps.tip: This is the whole dish. Undercooked tomato tastes raw and thin, and there is no onion here to hide behind.

steps.text: Add the water and salt, bring to a boil, then simmer 5 minutes.
Slide in the paneer cubes, add the sugar, and simmer very gently for 6 minutes, spooning gravy over them.
steps.tip: Never boil paneer hard — it tightens into rubber. A lazy bubble at the edge is all you want.

steps.text: Stir in the milk and the garam masala and warm through for 1 minute without boiling.
Take off the heat, scatter the coriander leaves and rest 5 minutes before serving with rice or roti.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat covered on a low flame with 3 tbsp water; the paneer firms up in the fridge and softens again as it warms.

recipes.name: Chungdi Malai
recipes.subtitle: prawns simmered in coconut milk, mildly spiced and faintly sweet, Odisha's most coaxing curry

ingredients.qty: 500g medium, shelled and deveined, tails on

ingredients.note: the traditional fat here; use oil if you prefer
for colour without heat

prepNotes: Rub the shelled prawns with 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt and rest 10 minutes. Rinse and pat dry before cooking.
Grind the onion to a smooth paste with no water. Wet onion paste will not brown properly and the gravy stays raw-tasting.
Shake the tin of coconut milk before opening, and keep it out of the fridge — cold coconut milk splits when it hits a hot pan.

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp ghee in a kadhai and sear the prawns on high for 45 seconds a side, until they just turn pink. Lift them out at once.
steps.tip: Prawns cook in under two minutes total. Anything more and they go to rubber, so undercook them here — they finish in the gravy.

steps.text: Add the remaining 2 tbsp ghee and drop in the bay leaves, cinnamon, cardamom and cloves. Fry 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the onion paste and fry on medium for 8-10 minutes, stirring often, until it turns pale gold and stops smelling raw.
steps.tip: This is the longest step and the one people cut short. Wait for the paste to pull away from the pan in a mass.

steps.text: Stir in the ginger and garlic pastes and cook 2 minutes more.
Add the turmeric, kashmiri chilli and salt with 2 tbsp water and fry 1 minute so the spices do not scorch.
Lower the flame and pour in the coconut milk. Add the sugar and slit green chillies.
steps.tip: Never boil coconut milk hard — it separates into oil and curds. Hold it at a bare simmer.

steps.text: Simmer gently, uncovered, for 6-8 minutes until the gravy thickens enough to coat a spoon.
Return the prawns with any juices, add the garam masala, and simmer 2 minutes only.
Take off the heat and rest 5 minutes covered before serving with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat on a low flame just until warm — reboiling both splits the coconut milk and toughens the prawns.

recipes.name: Dahi Pakhala
recipes.subtitle: Odia fermented rice in water with yogurt, eaten cold in the hot months

image.alt: Dahi pakhala, Odia fermented rice with yogurt

ingredients.note: day-old rice is traditional and better

prepNotes: Real pakhala is rice left in water overnight to ferment lightly, which gives it a faint sourness and, in the Odia summer, a cooling effect. The quick version below skips the overnight step.
For the traditional version, cover the cooked rice with water and leave it at room temperature 8-12 hours, then proceed from step 2.
Serve cold. This is a hot-weather dish and warm pakhala misses the point.

steps.text: Put the cooled rice in a bowl, add the water and lightly crush some of the grains with your fingers to cloud the liquid. For the traditional version, this is where you leave it overnight.
Whisk the yogurt smooth and stir it through with salt, the ginger and green chilli. It should be soupy, not thick; add more water if needed.
Heat the oil in a small pan. Splutter the mustard seeds, then add the dried chilli, curry leaves and asafoetida.
Pour the tempering over the pakhala, add a squeeze of lemon and scatter with coriander.
Chill at least 30 minutes before eating. Serve with something fried and salty alongside; fried fish, badi chura or a simple potato bharta are the usual partners.

recipes.storage: Eat the same day. The fermentation continues in the fridge and it turns increasingly sour after about 24 hours. Do not freeze.

recipes.name: Dalma
recipes.subtitle: Odia lentils simmered with vegetables, finished with roasted cumin and coconut

image.alt: A bowl of Odia dalma, lentils cooked with vegetables

ingredients.note: rinsed until the water runs clear
use oil to keep it vegan

prepNotes: Dalma has no onion or garlic at all. The flavour comes from the roasted cumin-chilli powder added at the end, so do not skip that step.
Cut the vegetables large. They should hold their shape in the finished dish rather than dissolve into the dal.

steps.text: Pressure cook the toor dal with turmeric, the ginger and 3 cups of water for 3 whistles, or simmer covered in a pot for about 35 minutes until completely soft.
Add the potato, raw banana, pumpkin and drumstick with a little more hot water and salt. Cook a further 2 whistles, or 12-15 minutes in a pot, until the vegetables are tender but not collapsing.
steps.tip: Add the tomato in the last five minutes so it keeps some shape.

steps.text: Meanwhile, dry roast half the cumin seeds and one dried chilli in a small pan over medium heat until the cumin darkens a shade and smells toasty, about 90 seconds. Cool, then grind to a coarse powder.
Heat the ghee in a small pan. Add the bay leaf, the remaining cumin seeds and the remaining dried chilli. When the cumin sizzles and turns fragrant, pour the whole tempering into the dal.
Stir in the grated coconut and the roasted cumin powder. Simmer 2 minutes so the flavours settle, then taste and adjust salt.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. It thickens considerably as it sits; loosen with hot water when reheating. Freezes well for a month, though the vegetables soften.

recipes.name: Ghanta Tarkari
recipes.subtitle: a big pot of mixed vegetables and chana dal with coconut, cooked for festivals without onion or garlic

ingredients.note: 1 tsp whole, 1/2 tsp for the coconut paste

prepNotes: Soak the chana dal at least 2 hours, or overnight if you can. It has to be tender at the same moment the vegetables are, and it is the slowest thing in the pot.
Grind 3 tbsp of the grated coconut with 1/2 tsp cumin seeds, half the ginger and 3 tbsp water to a coarse paste. Keep the last tablespoon of coconut back for finishing.
Rub your hands with oil before peeling the yam and colocasia to avoid itching.
Ghanta is a festival dish with no onion or garlic — cut the vegetables generously, it should look abundant.

steps.text: Boil the soaked chana dal in 400ml water with 1/2 tsp turmeric for 15 minutes, until it is just tender but still holds its shape. Do not drain.
steps.tip: Stop while the dal still has bite. It cooks another 15 minutes with the vegetables.

steps.text: Meanwhile heat the ghee in a large kadhai and add the bay leaves, whole cumin seeds and panch phoron. Let them crackle 20 seconds.
Add the remaining grated ginger and the slit green chillies and fry 1 minute.
Add the yam, colocasia and potato and fry 4 minutes until the cut faces turn golden.
Add the pumpkin, raw banana and drumstick with the remaining turmeric, the cumin powder and salt. Toss 2 minutes.
Pour in the remaining 500ml water, bring to a boil, cover and simmer 15 minutes.
Tip in the boiled chana dal with its water and the coconut-cumin paste. Stir gently from the bottom.
steps.tip: Stir with a light hand from here on — the pumpkin is ready to fall apart and it should not.

steps.text: Simmer uncovered 10 minutes until the gravy thickens and the yam is completely soft.
Mash a few pieces of pumpkin against the pan to bind the gravy, then stir in the garam masala.
Scatter the reserved fresh coconut over the top and rest 10 minutes off the heat before serving with rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and improves on day two as the dal and coconut settle. Reheat on the stovetop with 4 tbsp water, stirring as little as possible.

recipes.name: Khaja
recipes.subtitle: layered flaky pastry fried and dipped in sugar syrup, sold in stacks outside the Puri temple

ingredients.qty: 60g melted for the dough, plus 3 tbsp for the layering paste

ingredients.note: for the sata paste that makes the layers separate
for the syrup

ingredients.qty: 150ml for the dough, plus 200ml for the syrup

ingredients.note: or more ghee if you are being traditional

prepNotes: Rub the 60g melted ghee into the flour until a fistful holds its shape when squeezed. This moyan is what makes khaja short rather than hard.
Rest the dough a full 30 minutes under a damp cloth. Unrested dough springs back and the layers will not roll thin.
Beat the 3 tbsp ghee with the rice flour into a smooth white paste before you begin rolling — this sata is what separates the layers in the hot oil.
Make the syrup while the khaja fry so it is warm at the same moment they come out.

steps.text: Rub the melted ghee and salt into the maida for 3 minutes, then add the 150ml water a little at a time to make a firm, tight dough. Knead 6 minutes.
steps.tip: Firm, not soft. A slack dough will not hold its layers.

steps.text: Cover with a damp cloth and rest 30 minutes.
Beat the 3 tbsp ghee with the rice flour to a smooth, spreadable white paste.
Divide the dough in two. Roll each half into a thin rectangle about 2mm thick and spread the sata paste evenly right to the edges.
Roll each rectangle up tightly into a log, pressing as you go to expel air pockets.
steps.tip: Air pockets blow the layers apart in the oil. Roll tight and press along the seam.

steps.text: Cut each log into 2cm slices. Lay each slice cut-side up and press it flat with your palm, then roll very lightly into an oval about 8cm long — you should see the spiral of layers on the face.
Boil the 350g sugar with 200ml water and the cardamom for 8-10 minutes to a one-thread syrup, then keep it warm on the lowest flame.
steps.tip: One thread: a drop between thumb and finger pulls a single strand when you part them. Thicker and it will crystallise on the khaja.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a kadhai to low-medium — a scrap of dough should take a full 30 seconds to float up.
Fry the khaja in small batches for 7-9 minutes, turning often, until they are pale gold and the layers have visibly fanned open.
steps.tip: Low and slow is the entire technique. Fast frying browns the outside and leaves the inner layers doughy.

steps.text: Drain briefly, then dip each hot khaja in the warm syrup for 30 seconds, turning once, and lift onto a rack.
Leave to set for 30 minutes until the syrup coating turns matte and crisp.

recipes.storage: Keeps 10 days in an airtight tin at room temperature. Never refrigerate — the syrup weeps and the layers go soft.

recipes.name: Macha Besara
recipes.subtitle: rohu steaks in a hot, sour ground-mustard gravy, the Sunday fish curry of coastal Odisha

ingredients.qty: 600g rohu or katla, cut into 2cm-thick steaks
ingredients.note: any firm freshwater fish on the bone

ingredients.qty: 2 tbsp, soaked in warm water 20 minutes

ingredients.note: 3 for the paste, 2 sliced
1 tsp for rubbing the fish, 1/2 tsp for the gravy
4 for frying the fish, 1 for the gravy

prepNotes: Rub the fish steaks with 1 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and leave 15 minutes at room temperature. This firms the flesh so it does not break in the pan.
Soak the mustard seeds 20 minutes, then grind with 3 garlic cloves, 2 green chillies and a pinch of salt to a fine paste with 4 tbsp water.
Pat the fish dry just before frying. Wet fish sticks to the pan and tears when you turn it.

steps.text: Grind the soaked mustard, garlic, green chillies and a pinch of salt to a smooth paste with 4 tbsp water. Set aside.
Heat 4 tbsp mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes. Fry the turmeric-rubbed fish in one layer, 3 minutes a side, until a light crust forms.
steps.tip: Do not move the fish for the first 3 minutes. It releases from the pan on its own once the crust sets.

steps.text: Lift the fish out onto a plate. Pour off all but about 1 tbsp of the oil.
Add the panch phoron to the hot oil and let it crackle 20 seconds, then add the sliced garlic and 2 slit green chillies.
Add the chopped tomato with 1/2 tsp turmeric, the chilli powder and salt. Cook 6 minutes, mashing, until the tomato collapses and the oil separates.
Pour in the water and bring to a boil, then simmer 5 minutes.
Drop the flame to its lowest and stir in the mustard paste. Simmer uncovered 5 minutes without letting it boil.
steps.tip: A hard boil after the mustard goes in makes the gravy bitter. Keep it barely trembling.

steps.text: Slide the fried fish back in, spoon gravy over each piece, and simmer 4 minutes more.
Take off the heat, scatter the coriander leaves and rest 10 minutes before serving. The fish keeps absorbing gravy as it stands.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat on the lowest flame in a wide pan without stirring, tilting the pan to baste the fish instead; stirring breaks the steaks apart.

recipes.name: Mahura
recipes.subtitle: yam, pumpkin and colocasia in mustard with crumbled badi, the festival curry of western Odisha

ingredients.note: urad dal badi, the dried dumplings sold as 'bori' — fry them first
rounds off the mustard

prepNotes: Colocasia and yam make some hands itch. Rub your palms with a little mustard oil before peeling them, or wear gloves.
Soak the mustard seeds 20 minutes, then grind with 2 green chillies, the cumin seeds and a pinch of salt into a fine paste with 4 tbsp water.
Fry the badi first and set them aside — they go back in at the end so they stay chewy rather than dissolving.
This is a no-onion-garlic dish cooked for festivals and offerings; the mustard and jaggery carry all of it.

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp mustard oil and fry the crushed badi over medium heat for 2 minutes until deep brown and smelling nutty. Lift out and reserve.
steps.tip: Badi burn in seconds once they colour. Stand over them.

steps.text: Add the remaining 2 tbsp oil to the same kadhai and heat until it smokes, then lower the flame.
Add the panch phoron and let it crackle 20 seconds.
Add the yam, colocasia, potato and raw banana. Fry 4 minutes, turning, until the cut faces are lightly golden.
steps.tip: Colocasia goes slimy if it steams before it fries. Give it dry heat first.

steps.text: Add the pumpkin, slit green chilli, turmeric and salt and toss for 2 minutes.
Pour in the water, bring to a boil, cover and simmer 15 minutes until the yam is tender to a knife.
Turn the flame to its lowest, stir in the mustard paste and the jaggery, and simmer uncovered 8 minutes.
steps.tip: Keep it below a rolling boil or the mustard turns bitter.

steps.text: Return the fried badi, stir once and simmer 3 minutes more so they drink up the gravy but keep their bite.
Rest 5 minutes off the heat before serving with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat gently on the stovetop with a splash of water; the badi will be softer on day two, which many people prefer.

recipes.name: Rasabali
recipes.subtitle: fried chhena discs soaked in thick cardamom milk, the offering sweet of Kendrapara

ingredients.note: properly this is chhena from 2 litres of milk, drained but never pressed hard
for the rabri
100g for the milk, 50g for the syrup
binds the discs; this is wheat semolina, so the dish is not gluten-free
the traditional back-note; leave it out if you prefer
or a neutral oil, though ghee is traditional
for the light syrup

ingredients.qty: a pinch, soaked in 1 tbsp warm milk

prepNotes: The chhena must be fresh and soft. If you are using shop paneer, crumble it fine and knead it with the heel of your hand for a full 8 minutes until there is not a single lump and the mixture feels like dough.
Reduce the milk before you fry anything — it takes 30 minutes and cannot be hurried.
Rest the kneaded chhena dough 10 minutes covered before shaping. It shapes without cracking after resting.
Have the light sugar syrup made and warm before the discs come out of the ghee.

steps.text: Reduce the 1.5 litres of milk in a heavy pan over medium-low heat, scraping the sides down, for about 30 minutes until it has halved and thickened to a pourable rabri.
steps.tip: Scrape the skin off the sides back into the milk every few minutes. That is what gives rasabali its grain.

steps.text: Stir 100g sugar, the crushed cardamom, the pepper and the saffron milk into the reduced milk. Simmer 3 minutes and take off the heat.
Separately dissolve 50g sugar in 300ml water and bring to a boil to make a thin syrup. Keep it warm.
Knead the crumbled paneer with the rava for 8 minutes until smooth and dough-like, with no grains visible. Rest 10 minutes covered.
steps.tip: If the dough cracks when you flatten a ball, it needs more kneading, not more rava.

steps.text: Divide into 12 balls and flatten each into a disc about 5cm across and 1cm thick, with smooth unbroken edges.
Heat the ghee in a kadhai to medium-low — a scrap of dough should rise slowly and take 20 seconds to colour.
steps.tip: Hot ghee is the classic failure: the outside browns in seconds while the middle stays raw and the disc bursts.

steps.text: Fry the discs in batches, 4-5 minutes, turning once, until they are an even deep reddish-brown. They will puff slightly.
Drop each fried disc straight into the warm syrup and leave 10 minutes to soften and swell.
Lift the discs out, squeeze them very gently against the side of the bowl to shed excess syrup, and slide them into the warm rabri.
Rest at least 2 hours so the discs drink the milk all the way through. Serve cool, not chilled.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated in a covered box, and is better on day two. Serve cool or at room temperature; do not reheat, as the discs disintegrate.

recipes.name: Saga Bhaja
recipes.subtitle: amaranth greens stir-fried hard in mustard oil with garlic and dried chilli, done in ten minutes

ingredients.qty: 2 large bunches (about 400g), leaves and tender stems, chopped
ingredients.note: leutia saga; spinach works if you cannot get it

prepNotes: Wash the greens in three changes of water — amaranth holds grit in the leaf folds — then drain them properly and spread on a cloth for 10 minutes. Wet greens steam instead of frying.
Chop the stems separately from the leaves; the stems go in first.
Salt only at the very end. Salted greens release water immediately and you lose the fry.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a wide kadhai until it smokes, then lower the flame for 30 seconds.
Add the mustard seeds and let them pop, about 15 seconds.
Add the sliced garlic and broken red chillies and fry until the garlic is pale gold at the edges, about 1 minute.
steps.tip: Gold, not brown. Brown garlic will taste burnt against the greens.

steps.text: Throw in the chopped stems and the slit green chillies and fry 2 minutes on high.
Add the leaves in two handfuls, letting the first wilt before the second goes in. Keep the flame high.
Add the turmeric and stir-fry 4-5 minutes uncovered, tossing often, until the water the leaves throw off has cooked away.
steps.tip: Do not cover the pan at any point — trapped steam turns this into a soggy mash.

steps.text: Salt to taste, toss once more and take off the heat immediately.

recipes.storage: Eat within a few hours; greens dull and darken quickly. It keeps a day refrigerated but reheating makes it watery, so serve leftovers at room temperature.

recipes.name: Saja Pakhala
recipes.subtitle: same-day watered rice with lemon, ginger and a mustard tempering, eaten cool on the hottest afternoons

ingredients.note: Odia arua or any non-basmati short grain

ingredients.qty: 1.5 litres for cooking, plus 700ml cold for the pakhala

prepNotes: This is the fresh, curd-free version made and eaten the same day, not the overnight fermented basi pakhala.
Cook the rice loose and slightly soft, and do not drain away all the starch water — the torani is the point of the dish.
The rice must cool to room temperature before the cold water goes in. Hot rice makes a gluey pakhala.
Everything served alongside — fried fish, saga bhaja, a fried papad — should be salty and hot to contrast the cool rice.

steps.text: Boil the washed rice in 1.5 litres of water for 12-14 minutes, uncovered, until the grains are soft and just starting to swell open.
steps.tip: Cook it two minutes past what you would want for a normal plate of rice. Firm grains never soften once they are in cold water.
